lessons.title: Alarm cases: what it means and what you do next
lessons.body:
## A thirty-second algorithm

Every alarm opens the same way: **look at the patient, then look at the screen.** Not the other way around. A patient sitting up talking under a flat ECG trace has a lead problem. A grey, quiet patient under a perfect trace has a patient problem.

Then three questions, in order.

1. **Does the waveform match the number?** A heart rate of `180` over a jagged, unrecognizable trace is artifact. A heart rate of `180` over clean narrow complexes is a tachycardia.
2. **Is there a mechanical cause I can see and fix in thirty seconds?** Lead off, cuff on a moving arm, probe on a cold finger, tubing kinked, cable under tension.
3. **If not, escalate.** Parameter, value, trend, patient, room number.

> **Key:** Silencing is something you do after looking at a patient, never before. Silencing from the desk is making a clinical decision about someone you have not seen.

## The case set

| Alarm | What you see | Likely cause | Right move |
|---|---|---|---|
| Asystole | Patient eating lunch, one lead flat, the others normal | Electrode off | Replace it, re-prep the skin |
| Ventricular tachycardia | Patient brushing teeth, spikes matching the brushing rhythm | Motion artifact | Confirm the patient, stop the motion, verify in a second lead |
| Heart rate `210` | Palpated pulse `104`, trace shows very tall T waves | T wave double counting | Change the counting lead or adjust gain per policy, tell the nurse |
| SpO2 `82%` | Pleth flat and ragged, hands cold, patient talking in sentences | Poor perfusion at the probe | Warm the hand, change finger or move to the ear, recheck |
| SpO2 `88%` | Pleth clean, neck muscles working, three words at a time | Real hypoxemia | Oxygen per protocol and get the nurse now |
| BP `70/40` | Patient alert, arm was moving, last reading `128/76` | Motion during cycling | Repeat by hand before anyone acts |
| BP `70/40` | Patient grey and sleepy, skin cool, heart rate `126` | Real hypotension | Escalate first, confirm while help comes |
| Apnea | No impedance breaths, patient asleep and snoring loudly | Shallow breaths not detected | Look and count yourself |
| Low respiratory rate, sedated patient | Capnogram flat, no chest rise | Apnea | Jaw thrust, stimulate, call out |
| Repeated NIBP failure | Machine recycling with an error, patient shivering | Motion plus vasoconstriction | Manual pressure, warm the patient |

## The alarms that are never mechanical first

Three get treated as real until proven otherwise, because the cost of being wrong is enormous.

- **A new wide-complex tachycardia in a patient who does not look well.** Go now.
- **Any alarm on a patient who is not answering you.** The patient is the finding, not the monitor.
- **A capnography alarm on a sedated or intubated patient.** A flat trace is apnea or a disconnected airway until you have looked at the chest.

## Fixing the department's noise

Most false alarms trace to a handful of causes: dried-out electrodes, skin that was never prepped, cables under tension, a cuff one size too small, a probe on a cold hand. Changing electrodes daily and after defibrillation, prepping skin properly (dry it, wipe off oils, clip hair rather than shave), and leaving slack in every cable removes a large share of them.

> **On shift:** When you fix the cause of a false alarm, say so at handoff. "I changed his electrodes at 1400 because the V lead kept dropping" tells the next person the alarm history is clean now.

> **Trap:** Widening a limit to stop a mechanical alarm is hiding, not adjusting. The next real event falls inside the new limit and nothing sounds at all.
keyPoints: Look at the patient first and the screen second; the two together identify artifact in seconds.
Ask whether the waveform matches the number, then whether a mechanical cause is fixable in thirty seconds, then escalate.
The same value means different things: SpO2 88 with a clean pleth and accessory muscle use is real, with a flat pleth on a talking patient it is the probe.
Wide-complex tachycardia, an unresponsive patient, and a flat capnogram are treated as real before anything else.
Electrodes, skin prep, cable slack and cuff size account for most of a department's false alarms.

checks.q: The monitor alarms asystole. The patient is sitting up eating lunch, and one lead trace is flat while the others look normal. What do you do?
choices: Start compressions immediately
Silence the alarm from the desk and move on
Replace the electrode on the flat lead and re-prep the skin
Widen the low heart rate limit so it stops alarming
checks.why: A patient who is eating has a circulation. One flat lead among normal ones is an electrode problem, and fixing it at the source prevents the next twenty false alarms. Silencing without looking and widening limits both hide the problem instead of solving it.

checks.q: The monitor shows a heart rate of 210 while the radial pulse you palpate is 104, and the trace shows very tall T waves. What is happening?
choices: Supraventricular tachycardia with a pulse deficit
The monitor is counting each tall T wave as a second beat, doubling the displayed rate
The patient is in ventricular tachycardia
The SpO2 probe is interfering with the ECG
checks.why: A displayed rate exactly double a palpated rate, with tall T waves, is classic double counting. A real tachycardia at 210 would not give a regular palpable 104, and the oximeter does not affect ECG counting.

checks.q: A blood pressure alarms at 70/40 on a patient who is grey, cool and sleepy with a heart rate of 126. What is the first move?
choices: Repeat the cycle twice and see whether it corrects
Escalate immediately, then confirm manually while help is on the way
Move the cuff to the other arm and recycle
Silence the alarm and chart the reading
checks.why: The patient matches the number, which makes it real hypotension rather than artifact. Repeating cycles costs minutes in a patient who is already failing. Confirmation still happens, but it happens alongside escalation, not instead of it.

lessons.title: Telemetry troubleshooting: leads, artifact and the trace you cannot trust
lessons.body:
## What a lead actually shows

A monitoring lead is a **view** of the heart's electrical activity from one angle, not a picture of the heart. The monitor displays one or two of those views and counts the rate from one of them, so everything it reports depends on electrodes attached to clean, dry skin in the right places.

## Placement, three-lead and five-lead

A three-lead system gives you leads I, II and III.

- **White** on the **right** upper chest. White on right.
- **Black** on the left upper chest. Smoke over fire.
- **Red** on the left lower chest or abdomen.

Five-lead adds two.

- **Green** on the right lower chest or abdomen, the ground.
- **Brown** as the chest lead, usually placed at V1: fourth intercostal space just right of the sternum.

**Lead II** is the default display because it runs roughly parallel to the heart's normal electrical axis, which produces the tallest, clearest P waves and R waves and the most reliable rate counting. When the question is "is there a P wave?", lead II is where you look. When the question is whether a wide rhythm is ventricular, V1 helps most.

Electrodes go on flat, relatively bony areas, off large muscle bellies and off breast tissue, so movement does not corrupt the trace.

## Skin prep is most of the job

Most bad traces are skin, not equipment.

1. Dry the skin. Sweat and lotion break the electrical contact.
2. Wipe oils off with alcohol and let it dry, or use the abrasive tab on the electrode packet.
3. **Clip** chest hair rather than shaving. Hair holds the electrode off the skin, and a razor makes micro-cuts.
4. Check the gel. A dried-out electrode looks perfectly fine and works badly.
5. Change electrodes at least every `24 hours`, and after defibrillation, heavy sweating or a shower.
6. Leave slack in the cable and secure it so patient movement pulls on tape, not on the electrode.

> **Key:** A clean trace is built on prepped skin and slack cables. Everything else is downstream of those two things.

## Reading artifact

| Appearance | Usual cause |
|---|---|
| Slow rolling drift of the baseline | Loose electrode, respiration, patient movement |
| Fine rapid fuzz along the baseline | Muscle tremor, shivering, anxiety, Parkinson tremor |
| Regular sharp spikes about `60` times per second | Electrical interference or a poor ground |
| A trace that looks exactly like ventricular tachycardia in a patient who feels fine | Rhythmic motion artifact: brushing teeth, tapping, scratching |
| One flat lead, the others normal | That electrode is off |
| All leads flat with the patient talking | Cable disconnected at the monitor or the patient module |

One question resolves nearly all of it: **does the patient match the trace?** Feel a pulse while you watch the screen. If the rate you feel and the rate you see disagree, the screen is wrong.

## The other telemetry problems

**Double counting.** A tall T wave or a pacer spike is counted as an extra beat and the displayed rate doubles. Change which lead the monitor counts from or adjust the gain per policy, and tell the nurse.

**Undercounting.** Low-voltage complexes from obesity, emphysema or a pericardial effusion are too small to count, so the reported rate is lower than the patient's real rate.

**Signal loss on a mobile telemetry patient.** Out of range, dead battery, patient in the bathroom, patient off the unit for imaging. Lost telemetry is not a technical curiosity. It means nobody is watching.

> **On shift:** When a monitored patient leaves for imaging, somebody owns the monitoring. Say out loud who is going and which monitor they are on.
keyPoints: White on right, smoke over fire, red below; green is the ground and brown is the chest lead, usually at V1.
Lead II is the default because it parallels the heart's axis, giving the clearest P waves and the most reliable rate count.
Most bad traces are skin: dry it, remove oils, clip rather than shave, and change electrodes every 24 hours and after defibrillation.
Feel a pulse while watching the screen; if the rates disagree, the screen is wrong.
A tall T wave or a pacer spike can be double counted and double the displayed rate; low-voltage complexes can be undercounted.

checks.q: Where is the brown chest electrode usually placed on a five-lead system?
choices: Fourth intercostal space just to the right of the sternum, the V1 position
Left mid-axillary line at the sixth rib
Right upper chest below the clavicle
Left lower abdomen
checks.why: The brown lead is the single chest lead and it is conventionally placed at V1, which is most useful for distinguishing wide-complex rhythms. The other positions describe the white, red and defibrillation pad locations.

checks.q: Why is lead II the usual default display on a bedside monitor?
choices: It is the only lead a three-electrode system can produce
It runs roughly parallel to the heart's normal electrical axis, giving the tallest clearest P and R waves and the best rate counting
It is least affected by patient movement
It shows ST changes better than any other lead
checks.why: Lead II aligns with the direction of normal depolarization, so complexes are upright and tall and the monitor counts them accurately. Three-lead systems produce I, II and III, and lead II has no special advantage for motion or ST analysis.

checks.q: A monitored patient goes to CT and the telemetry signal is lost for 20 minutes. How should this be treated?
choices: As expected downtime that needs no action
As a battery problem to fix when the patient returns
As a period in which nobody was monitoring the patient, which must be reported and covered by a named person with a transport monitor
As a reason to discontinue telemetry
checks.why: A gap in telemetry on a monitored patient is a gap in care, not a technical detail. Someone must accompany the patient with a working transport monitor, and the gap is communicated rather than quietly absorbed.

lessons.title: Capnography cases: shapes, sedation, asthma and shock
lessons.body:
## The waveform has parts, and each part fails differently

| Phase | What it is | What a problem looks like |
|---|---|---|
| I, baseline | Dead-space gas with no CO2, should sit at zero | A baseline above zero means rebreathing: exhausted absorber, faulty valve, or too little fresh gas |
| II, upstroke | Alveolar gas arriving, should be steep | A slurred, sloping upstroke means obstruction to flow |
| III, plateau | Alveolar gas, nearly flat, ending at the end-tidal value | An upsloping plateau means uneven emptying, classically bronchospasm |
| 0, downstroke | Inhalation, should fall sharply to zero | A slow return suggests a leak or a sampling problem |

A **curare cleft**, a notch dipping down in the middle of the plateau, is a paralyzed patient beginning to breathe as the blockade wears off.

## Obstruction: the shark fin, quantified

In asthma and COPD the upstroke slurs into the plateau and the whole shape rounds into a fin. Two things make it useful.

First, it changes **before the patient reports feeling better**. A fin that squares off during a bronchodilator treatment is objective improvement. A fin that stays rounded through three treatments is a patient who is not responding.

Second, the number moves in a pattern. Early in an attack the patient blows off CO2 with a fast rate, so EtCO2 is **low**, often `25-30 mmHg`. As the patient tires, EtCO2 **rises toward and past normal**. A `40 mmHg` reading in a severe asthmatic still working hard is not reassurance; it is a patient heading into respiratory failure.

> **Trap:** A normalizing end-tidal number in a tiring asthmatic is one of the most dangerous reassuring numbers in the department. Read it with the work of breathing, never alone.

## Sedation

Nasal-cannula sampling capnography on a sedated patient shows apnea within seconds, long before the pulse oximeter, especially on supplemental oxygen where saturation can hold for a minute after breathing stops.

Three patterns, in the order they usually develop:

- **Rising EtCO2 with a slowing rate.** Hypoventilation, the signature of opioid effect. This is the warning, and stimulation and a coached deep breath usually fix it.
- **A low, blunted, irregular waveform.** Partial airway obstruction. Reposition, chin lift, jaw thrust.
- **A flat line.** Apnea, or a displaced sampling cannula. Look at the chest before you troubleshoot the equipment.

## Shock, output, and arrest

Because EtCO2 depends on blood carrying CO2 to the lungs, it falls when cardiac output falls even when the lungs are working perfectly.

- A low EtCO2 in a patient with a normal rate and clear lungs raises the question of poor perfusion: hemorrhage, sepsis, pulmonary embolism.
- A **sudden drop** in EtCO2 in an intubated, ventilated patient with no circuit change means blood is not reaching the lungs. Massive pulmonary embolism or a sudden loss of cardiac output until proven otherwise.
- In arrest the number is direct feedback on the compressions: under `10 mmHg` means push harder and faster with full recoil, and swap the compressor.

## Low EtCO2 with a fast rate in a sick patient

A patient breathing `32` times a minute with an EtCO2 of `18 mmHg` and clear lungs is deliberately blowing off CO2 to compensate for a metabolic acidosis. Diabetic ketoacidosis, sepsis with a high lactate, salicylate toxicity and severe kidney failure all produce it.

The low number here is not a ventilation failure. It is the body's answer to an acid problem, and the patient is working extremely hard to produce it. When that patient starts to tire and the EtCO2 climbs back toward normal, the acidosis has not improved; the compensation has failed.

> **Key:** EtCO2 answers three questions at once: is air moving, is blood moving, and is the metabolism normal. Which question it is answering depends on the rest of the patient.
keyPoints: The capnogram has four phases: a baseline above zero means rebreathing, an upsloping plateau means obstruction.
A curare cleft in the plateau means a paralyzed patient is starting to breathe again.
In asthma EtCO2 starts low and rises toward normal as the patient tires, which is deterioration, not improvement.
In sedation, rising EtCO2 with a slowing rate is the opioid warning; a flat trace is apnea until you have looked at the chest.
A sudden EtCO2 drop with no circuit change means blood is not reaching the lungs.

checks.q: A severe asthmatic arrives with an EtCO2 of 26 mmHg. Forty minutes later, still working hard with accessory muscles, his EtCO2 is 41 mmHg. What does this mean?
choices: He is improving, since the value is now normal
The sampling line has become obstructed
He is tiring and heading toward respiratory failure; a normalizing number here is a danger sign
He has developed a metabolic alkalosis
checks.why: Early asthma drives EtCO2 low by hyperventilation. A rise back to normal while the patient still works hard means the ventilation that was holding the number down is failing. The number looks better precisely as the patient gets worse.

checks.q: An intubated, ventilated patient's EtCO2 falls suddenly from 38 to 12 mmHg. The circuit is intact, the tube is at the same depth, and the waveform still has a normal shape. What does this suggest?
choices: A sudden loss of pulmonary blood flow, such as a massive pulmonary embolism or loss of cardiac output
Esophageal intubation
Bronchospasm
Rebreathing of exhaled gas
checks.why: A preserved waveform shape with a collapsed value means ventilation continues but perfusion has failed, so little CO2 is being delivered to the lungs. Esophageal placement gives no waveform, bronchospasm slurs the shape, and rebreathing raises the baseline.

checks.q: A notch appears dipping downward in the middle of the plateau of a ventilated patient's capnogram. What does it represent?
choices: A leak in the sampling line
A curare cleft: the patient is beginning to breathe as neuromuscular blockade wears off
Bronchospasm
Cardiac oscillation artifact requiring no action
checks.why: The cleft is the patient's own inspiratory effort interrupting the machine breath, so it signals returning respiratory drive and the need to reassess sedation and paralysis. A leak affects the downstroke and bronchospasm slurs the upstroke.

lessons.title: Sepsis hour by hour: the first six hours at the bedside
lessons.body:
## Why sepsis is run as a clock

Sepsis kills by time. Every hour between the moment a patient is septic and the moment antibiotics reach them raises mortality measurably. That is why sepsis is run as a timed bundle rather than a diagnose-then-treat sequence, and why departments track the clock from the moment the first concerning set of numbers is recorded.

That clock usually starts at **triage**, not at the physician's diagnosis. Which is one reason a technician's vital signs matter as much as they do.

## 0 to 15 minutes: recognition

The screen is made of numbers you already take. Temperature over `38 C` or under `36 C`, heart rate over `90`, respiratory rate over `20`, with a suspected source. Or qSOFA: respiratory rate `22` or more, altered mentation, systolic `100` or less, two of three.

Your tasks: a full and honest set with a **counted** respiratory rate, a temperature by a route that is actually accurate (a core or rectal reading when the patient is cold or shocked and the oral number looks wrong), a point-of-care glucose, and saying the numbers out loud to the nurse.

Then: monitor on, two large-bore IVs at `18 gauge` or larger, and a bed where the patient can be watched.

> **Key:** Your first set of vitals starts the clock. A guessed respiratory rate of 18 on a patient breathing 26 delays everything that follows it.

## 15 to 60 minutes: the hour-1 bundle

Five items, targeted within an hour of recognition.

1. **Measure lactate.** An elevated lactate means tissue is not getting the oxygen it needs.
2. **Blood cultures before antibiotics.** Two sets from two sites, drawn before the drug unless drawing them would meaningfully delay it.
3. **Broad-spectrum antibiotics.** The most time-sensitive item on the list.
4. **`30 mL/kg` crystalloid** for hypotension or a lactate of `4 mmol/L` or higher. In an `80 kg` adult that is `2400 mL`, and it runs through large IVs under a pressure bag, not by gravity through a `22 gauge`.
5. **Vasopressors** if the mean arterial pressure stays under `65 mmHg` despite the fluid.

In practice most of that list is physically done by a technician: the IVs, the cultures, the point-of-care lactate, the fluid hung and pressure-bagged, the catheter if output measurement is ordered, and the vitals through all of it.

## 1 to 3 hours: is it working?

Reassessment is the step that gets skipped.

- **Repeat the lactate** if the first was over `2 mmol/L`. Clearance is the marker. A lactate falling from `4.2` to `2.6` is a patient responding; one that rises is a patient who is not.
- **Mean arterial pressure at least `65 mmHg`.** Remember that the monitor measures the mean directly and calculates the systolic, so in shock the mean is the number to trust.
- **Urine output at least `0.5 mL/kg/h`**, roughly `30 mL/h` in an average adult. Measure it hourly and report it.
- **Reassess perfusion with your hands:** skin temperature at the knees, capillary refill, mottling, mental status. These move before the numbers do, in both directions.

## 3 to 6 hours: pressors, source, destination

If pressure will not hold, norepinephrine is the usual first vasopressor and it wants a reliable line. **Source control** is the half of sepsis care that is easy to forget while everyone watches numbers: an abscess drained, an infected line pulled, an obstructed kidney decompressed, dead bowel resected. Antibiotics do not work around an undrained source.

By now disposition is usually decided. Your handoff carries the **timeline**, not just the current numbers: when the clock started, when antibiotics actually went in, how much fluid has genuinely infused, what the lactates were and when, and the total urine output.

> **On shift:** The number people forget to hand off is how much of the `30 mL/kg` actually ran. A bag hung is not a bag infused.

> **Trap:** A septic patient who becomes calm and stops complaining has not improved. Falling agitation with a rising heart rate is a brain running out of perfusion.
keyPoints: The sepsis clock usually starts at triage, so the first set of vital signs is what launches everything.
Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, pressors for a MAP under 65.
30 mL/kg is about 2400 mL in an 80 kg adult and needs large-bore access and a pressure bag, not gravity.
Reassess at 1-3 hours: repeat lactate for clearance, MAP 65, urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h, and hands-on perfusion signs.
Hand off the timeline, especially how much fluid actually infused, not only the latest numbers.

checks.q: An 80 kg patient needs 30 mL/kg of crystalloid for septic hypotension. How much is that, and how should it run?
choices: 800 mL, by gravity through any working IV
2400 mL, through large-bore access under a pressure bag or rapid infuser
3000 mL, over the next 6 hours
1600 mL, through a central line only
checks.why: 30 mL/kg times 80 kg is 2400 mL and it is meant to go in quickly, which small-bore gravity infusion cannot achieve. The volume is not weight-independent, it is not a six-hour infusion, and peripheral large-bore access is entirely adequate.

checks.q: The nurse is about to hang antibiotics for a suspected septic patient and the blood cultures have not been drawn. Drawing them would take about two minutes. What do you say?
choices: Nothing; antibiotics are the most time-sensitive item
Speak up now, because cultures drawn after antibiotics are far less likely to grow the organism, and two minutes does not meaningfully delay the drug
Suggest drawing the cultures an hour after the antibiotics
Suggest sending a urine culture instead
checks.why: Antibiotics sterilize the blood within minutes, so post-antibiotic cultures often lose the organism and with it the ability to narrow therapy. The bundle accepts giving antibiotics first only when obtaining cultures would cause a meaningful delay, which two minutes is not.

checks.q: A septic patient who was restless and complaining an hour ago is now quiet and easy to manage. His heart rate has gone from 104 to 128. What does this most likely represent?
choices: A response to the fluids and antibiotics
Worsening perfusion of the brain; falling agitation with a rising heart rate is deterioration
The effect of the analgesia he received
Normal fatigue after a long wait
checks.why: Improvement lowers the heart rate; here it is rising, so the settling is a falling level of consciousness rather than comfort. Attributing new quietness to analgesia or fatigue is the classic way this deterioration is missed.

lessons.title: Neuro checks, deep: pupils, GCS trends and the NIHSS you will hear
lessons.body:
## Glasgow Coma Scale, component by component

GCS is three separate scales added together, and reporting the components is far more useful than reporting the total.

**Eye opening (E), 1 to 4.** `4` spontaneous, `3` to speech, `2` to pain, `1` none.

**Verbal (V), 1 to 5.** `5` oriented, `4` confused conversation, `3` inappropriate words, `2` incomprehensible sounds, `1` none. An intubated patient is scored `1T` or reported as not testable.

**Motor (M), 1 to 6.** `6` obeys commands, `5` localizes pain, `4` withdraws from pain, `3` abnormal flexion (decorticate), `2` extension (decerebrate), `1` none.

Total `3` to `15`. A GCS of `8` or less is the classic threshold at which the airway is considered unprotected.

The scoring rules that get missed: score the **best** response any limb gives; test pain centrally, with a trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure, because a spinal reflex can move a limb with no brain involved; and report the breakdown, because "E3 V4 M6, total 13" tells a clinician much more than "13".

> **Trap:** Motor `5` (localizes: reaches toward the stimulus and tries to push it away) and motor `4` (withdraws: simply pulls away) are the most confused pair on the scale, and they are the difference between an intact cortex and an impaired one.

## The pupil exam

Dim the room, have the patient look into the distance so they are not accommodating, and bring the light in from the side.

Record three things per eye: **size in millimetres**, **shape**, and **reaction** (brisk, sluggish, none). Then check the **consensual** response: light in one eye should constrict both.

| Finding | Common meaning |
|---|---|
| One dilated, sluggish or fixed pupil | Third nerve compression from rising pressure on that side; an emergency |
| Both pinpoint and reactive | Opioids, or a pontine lesion |
| Both mid-position and fixed | Midbrain injury |
| Both dilated and fixed | Severe hypoxia or ischemia, some drugs, atropine |
| Unequal but both briskly reactive in a well patient | Physiologic anisocoria, present in roughly `20%` of people |

A new asymmetry, a newly sluggish pupil, or any pupil that has changed since the last check is reported the moment you see it, not at the end of the round.

## NIHSS: what the number means

You will not be scoring the NIH Stroke Scale, but you will hear it and chart around it. It has `11` items: level of consciousness and orientation, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, arm and leg motor strength, limb ataxia, sensation, language, speech clarity, and extinction or neglect. Totals run `0` to `42`.

Rough interpretation: `0` no stroke signs, `1-4` minor, `5-15` moderate, `16-20` moderate to severe, `21` and above severe. It is repeated deliberately, because the change matters more than the entry number.

What you can recognize without scoring anything: a facial droop that spares the forehead, one arm drifting down when both are held out, slurred speech, words coming out wrong or not at all, gaze pulled to one side, and a patient ignoring one half of the world. **Time of last known well** is the single most important piece of history in the room, and it is worth confirming with family yourself.

## Trending, and what a change means

A neuro check is only useful against the last one, so it is recorded the same way every time by whoever performs it.

- A **drop of 2 or more GCS points** is reported immediately.
- A **new pupil asymmetry** is reported immediately.
- After thrombolytics, checks and blood pressure run every `15 minutes` for `2 hours`, then every `30 minutes` for `6 hours`, then hourly, with blood pressure held under roughly `180/105`.
- **New severe headache, nausea and vomiting, sudden hypertension, or any decline** during that watch means bleeding into the brain until imaging says otherwise. Stop, get the nurse, stay with the patient.

> **Key:** Report components and times, not adjectives. "E2 V2 M4 at 0910, was E3 V4 M6 at 0855" is an emergency anyone can act on. "He seems worse" is not.
keyPoints: GCS is E 1-4, V 1-5, M 1-6 for a total of 3-15; report the components and times, not just the total.
Localizing (M5) reaches toward the stimulus; withdrawal (M4) only pulls away, and the difference is cortical function.
Record pupil size in millimetres, shape, reaction and consensual response; new asymmetry is reported immediately.
NIHSS has 11 items and runs 0-42; repeated scores matter more than the first, and last known well is the critical history.
After thrombolytics: checks every 15 minutes for 2 hours, blood pressure under about 180/105, and new headache or vomiting means bleeding until proven otherwise.

checks.q: A patient with a head injury opens his eyes to your voice, gives confused answers, and reaches up toward your hand when you pinch his trapezius. What is his GCS?
choices: E4 V5 M6, total 15
E3 V4 M5, total 12
E2 V3 M4, total 9
E3 V3 M4, total 10
checks.why: Eyes opening to speech is E3, confused conversation is V4, and reaching toward the stimulus is localizing, which is M5. Withdrawal would only pull away without reaching, which would be M4 and a lower total.

checks.q: Ninety minutes into a post-thrombolytic watch, a stroke patient develops a sudden severe headache, vomits, and becomes drowsy. What do you do?
choices: Give an antiemetic and recheck in 15 minutes
Lower the head of the bed and let him rest
Stop, stay with the patient and get the nurse immediately, because this is intracranial bleeding until imaging says otherwise
Document it and include it in the next scheduled check
checks.why: New headache, vomiting and declining consciousness after thrombolytics is the presentation of intracranial hemorrhage, which needs the drug stopped, urgent imaging and blood pressure control. Treating the symptom or waiting for the next scheduled check loses the time that matters.

checks.q: You find that a patient's right pupil is now 6 mm and sluggish while the left is 3 mm and brisk. An hour ago both were 3 mm and brisk. What does this mean?
choices: Physiologic anisocoria, which is common and benign
A new unilateral dilated sluggish pupil suggests rising pressure compressing the third nerve, and it is reported immediately
An expected effect of the analgesia given
Eye drops given during the eye exam
checks.why: The key word is new. Physiologic anisocoria is present at baseline and both pupils react briskly, and opioids constrict rather than dilate. A pupil that has changed since the last documented check is an emergency finding.

lessons.title: Twelve patients who are sliding: reading deterioration
lessons.body:
## How to read this

Twelve patterns, each one built the same way: the finding is ordinary, the numbers are almost normal, and the right move is to say it out loud with the trend attached. Read the left column, decide, then read across.

## The twelve

| What you see | What it means | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 1. `68F`, pneumonia. Respiratory rate `18`, then `22`, then `26` over 45 minutes; everything else stable | Respiratory rate is the earliest warning and it is moving one direction | Report all three values with times and ask the nurse to look |
| 2. `54M`, GI bleed. Heart rate `110`, systolic `108`, both inside alarm limits | Shock index `1.0`, compensated shock hiding behind two acceptable numbers | Report the shock index alongside the active bleed |
| 3. `72F`, abdominal pain. Pressures run `128/72`, `118/80`, `106/88` | Narrowing pulse pressure: vasoconstricting to defend a falling volume | Report the trend, not the last systolic |
| 4. `45M`, sedated for a reduction. Capnogram flat for three breaths, SpO2 `99%` on oxygen | Apnea, with oxygen masking it | Jaw thrust, stimulate, call out; do not wait for the oximeter |
| 5. `81M`, hip fracture, agreeable all morning, now cannot name the month | New confusion is a vital sign | Report it as a change, with what he could do an hour ago |
| 6. `30F`, asthma. Was wheezing loudly, chest now quiet and she is sleepy | A silent chest in asthma is no air moving, not improvement | Emergency; get help into the room now |
| 7. `60M`, chest pain, cool and clammy with a normal blood pressure | Diaphoresis without fever is a catecholamine surge | Report skin findings next to the vitals |
| 8. `2y`, bronchiolitis. Heart rate `168` for an hour, now `72` and floppy | Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia and a pre-arrest sign | Call for help, oxygen, prepare to resuscitate |
| 9. `77F`, urosepsis. Knees mottled, capillary refill `4 seconds`, systolic `104` | Peripheral shutdown before the pressure falls | Escalate; spreading mottling is a poor-outcome marker |
| 10. `58M`, post-thrombolytic stroke, sudden severe headache and vomiting | Intracranial hemorrhage until imaging says otherwise | Stop, stay with him, get the nurse now |
| 11. `40F`, sickle cell crisis, asks to be left to sleep 20 minutes after opioids | Withdrawal into sleep in acute illness is falling consciousness, and opioids depress breathing | Count the rate and check capnography before letting her sleep |
| 12. `65M`, day 1 alcohol withdrawal. Heart rate `124`, tremor, sweating, now seeing bugs | Withdrawal escalating toward delirium tremens, which carries real mortality | Report the trend and the hallucinations; this needs treatment now |

## The thread running through all twelve

None of these patients set off a monitor alarm at the moment it mattered. In every case the finding was a **trend**, a **physical sign**, or a **change in behavior**, and in every case the alarm limits were still satisfied.

Three habits catch all twelve.

1. Compare with the last set, every time, before you chart.
2. Touch the patient. Skin temperature, capillary refill, mottling and diaphoresis are free, fast and early.
3. Ask one question that requires thought rather than a yes or a no. "What month is it?" catches what "Are you okay?" never will.

> **Key:** A monitor alarms on a value. A person notices a direction. That difference is most of the reason this job exists.

> **Trap:** Two of the twelve look like improvement: the asthmatic whose chest goes quiet, and the patient who finally settles and wants to sleep. Both are deterioration, and both are commonly charted as "resting comfortably".
keyPoints: Deterioration usually shows as a trend, a physical sign or a behavior change while every alarm limit is still satisfied.
Shock index over 0.9 and a narrowing pulse pressure both flag compensated shock behind acceptable-looking numbers.
A silent chest in asthma and a patient who suddenly wants to sleep are deterioration disguised as improvement.
Touch the patient every round: skin temperature, capillary refill, mottling and diaphoresis are earlier than the monitor.
Ask one question that requires thought; new confusion is a vital sign in its own right.

checks.q: A 30-year-old asthmatic who has been wheezing loudly for an hour now has a quiet chest and is getting sleepy. What does this mean?
choices: The bronchodilators have worked and she can be moved to a lower acuity area
She is no longer moving enough air to make a wheeze, which is impending respiratory failure
She is simply tired from the work of breathing
The stethoscope placement is wrong
checks.why: Wheeze requires turbulent airflow, so losing it while the patient deteriorates means airflow has collapsed. Sleepiness in an asthmatic is carbon dioxide retention, not rest. This is one of the classic false-improvement patterns in emergency medicine.

checks.q: A 54-year-old with a GI bleed has a heart rate of 110 and a systolic of 108, both within the set alarm limits. What should you calculate and report?
choices: Mean arterial pressure, which is normal
Pulse pressure, which is wide
Shock index of 1.0, which indicates compensated shock despite two acceptable-looking numbers
Nothing; both values are within limits
checks.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic; 110 over 108 is about 1.0, well above the 0.9 threshold that predicts serious illness and transfusion need. Each number alone looks tolerable, which is exactly why the ratio is useful.

checks.q: Which habit catches the most deterioration that the monitor misses?
choices: Comparing each set of vitals with the previous one before charting, and touching the patient every round
Narrowing all alarm limits to the tightest possible settings
Charting vitals more frequently without reviewing them
Relying on the monitor's trend graph rather than physical findings
checks.why: Deterioration is a direction, and direction only appears when you compare sets. Physical findings like mottling, cool skin and confusion precede monitor changes. Tighter limits only add false alarms, and recording numbers nobody reads changes nothing.

lessons.title: Pediatric monitoring: a case set
lessons.body:
## Look before you touch

Before any number, three things from the doorway.

1. **Appearance.** Tone, interactivity, consolability, gaze, speech or cry. A floppy baby who does not track you is sick whatever the numbers say.
2. **Work of breathing.** Nasal flaring, grunting, head bobbing, retractions between the ribs, below the ribs and above the sternum, tripoding, stridor or wheeze audible without a stethoscope.
3. **Circulation to the skin.** Pale, mottled or blue. Check capillary refill centrally, at the chest or the kneecap, not on a cold foot.

Any one of the three abnormal means a sick child. All three abnormal is a resuscitation.

## Numbers with a pediatric twist

**Hypotension by age.** Systolic below `70 + (2 x age in years)` is hypotension between `1` and `10` years, so a `4`-year-old is hypotensive under `78`. Under `90` from `10` years up, under `70` for infants, under `60` for neonates.

**Bradycardia is hypoxia** until proven otherwise. In an infant, a heart rate under `100` with poor perfusion is an indication to begin compressions under most protocols, because a slow heart in a hypoxic child is the step immediately before arrest.

**Cuff size** follows the adult rule: the bladder spans about `40%` of the arm width and `80-100%` of its circumference. An adult cuff on a child's arm reads falsely low and manufactures false reassurance.

**SpO2 probe** goes on a toe, a foot, or a wrapped hand in infants. Motion is the main enemy, so a settled child on a parent's chest gives a better trace than a fighting child on a stretcher.

**Weight in kilograms** is measured or taken from a length-based tape. Every dose and every piece of equipment depends on it.

## The case set

| Presentation | The finding that matters | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| `6 mo`, bronchiolitis, rate `70`, grunting, head bobbing | Grunting is the child generating their own positive pressure | Severe distress; do not leave the bedside |
| `3 y`, croup, stridor only when crying | Stridor **at rest** is the escalation | Keep him calm on a parent's lap; agitation worsens obstruction |
| `2 y`, gastroenteritis, heart rate `170`, alert, refill `3 sec`, BP `92/60` | Tachycardia with a normal pressure is compensated shock | Report now; the pressure holds until suddenly it does not |
| `10 mo`, fever, heart rate `190` with no beat-to-beat variability | A fixed rate this high raises SVT rather than sinus tachycardia | Get a rhythm strip and a clinician |
| `4 y` asthmatic, was wheezing loudly, now quiet and sleepy | Silent chest plus a sleepy child | Impending respiratory failure |
| `8 y`, appendicitis, heart rate `118`, BP `104/70`, insists he is fine | Children minimize and compensate; the rate is the honest number | Trend it and report it |
| Newborn, heart rate `78`, blue, floppy | Bradycardia in a neonate is hypoxia | Ventilate first, then reassess; this is a resuscitation |
| `5 y`, seizure has stopped, now snoring with SpO2 `88%` | Post-ictal airway obstruction from the tongue and soft tissue | Reposition, suction, oxygen, and stay there |

> **Key:** In children the heart rate tells the truth and the blood pressure lies until the very end. Treat a fast, poorly perfused child as being in shock even with a normal pressure.

> **Trap:** A normal heart rate in a child who looks terrible is not reassurance. It can be the brief passage between tachycardia and bradycardia.

## Comfort as measurement technique

An upset child gives unusable numbers: motion artifact on the pleth, a fictional impedance respiratory rate, and a blood pressure taken mid-scream. A child settled on a parent's chest and distracted gives real data. Comfort here is not only kindness, it is how you get a measurement worth charting.
keyPoints: Assess appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin from the doorway before touching any equipment.
Pediatric hypotension is systolic below 70 plus twice the age in years, between 1 and 10 years old.
Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise and is a pre-arrest sign.
Grunting, head bobbing, nasal flaring and stridor at rest all mark severe distress.
A calm, comfortable child produces accurate numbers; an upset one produces artifact.

checks.q: A 4-year-old with gastroenteritis has a systolic blood pressure of 76. Is this hypotension?
choices: No, anything above 70 is acceptable at any age
Yes: the threshold is 70 plus twice the age in years, which is 78 at age 4
No, the adult threshold of 90 does not apply to children
It cannot be determined without a mean arterial pressure
checks.why: The formula 70 plus 2 times age gives 78 for a 4-year-old, so 76 is below it and represents hypotension, which in a child is a very late finding. The flat 70 and adult 90 thresholds apply to infants and to children over 10 respectively.

checks.q: A 2-year-old with bronchiolitis has had a heart rate of 165 for an hour. It is now 72 and he is limp. What does this represent?
choices: Improvement as the child settles and tires
A vagal response to suctioning
Hypoxia causing bradycardia, which is a pre-arrest sign requiring immediate help and oxygen
Sinus arrhythmia, which is normal at this age
checks.why: A child compensates with tachycardia until oxygen runs out, at which point the rate crashes. Bradycardia plus poor tone in a hypoxic child is the step before arrest, and it is treated as a resuscitation, not as a child who has calmed down.

checks.q: A 3-year-old with croup has stridor only when he cries. What is the right approach?
choices: Keep him calm on a parent's lap, since agitation worsens airway obstruction, and watch for stridor at rest
Lay him flat and examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Separate him from the parent so he can be monitored properly
Treat it as mild and move him to the waiting room
checks.why: Crying increases airflow turbulence and swelling in a narrowed airway, so calm is therapeutic. Stridor at rest marks escalation and is what you are watching for. Throat examination in a child with stridor risks precipitating obstruction, and he still needs observation.

lessons.title: Monitoring the sedated patient: RASS, Aldrete and getting to discharge
lessons.body:
## Two scales, two different questions

**RASS**, the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale, answers "how deep is this patient right now?"

| Score | What you see |
|---|---|
| `+4` | Combative, violent, a danger to staff |
| `+3` | Very agitated, pulling at lines or tubes |
| `+2` | Agitated, frequent non-purposeful movement |
| `+1` | Restless and anxious but not aggressive |
| `0` | Alert and calm |
| `-1` | Drowsy, holds eye contact over `10 seconds` to voice |
| `-2` | Light sedation, brief waking to voice, eye contact under `10 seconds` |
| `-3` | Moderate sedation, movement or eye opening to voice but no eye contact |
| `-4` | Deep sedation, no response to voice, movement to physical stimulation |
| `-5` | Unarousable to voice or physical stimulation |

How you score it: observe for `10 seconds`. If the patient is not alert, say their name and ask them to open their eyes and look at you. If there is still nothing, shake the shoulder, then rub the sternum. The level at which they respond is the score.

Most sedated emergency department patients are targeted at `0 to -2`, drowsy but rousable, because deeper sedation prolongs ventilation and worsens outcomes.

**Aldrete** answers a different question: "is this patient recovered enough to leave?" Five items, `0-2` each, out of `10`.

| Item | 2 points | 1 point | 0 points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Activity | Moves all four limbs on command | Moves two limbs | Moves none |
| Respiration | Breathes deeply and coughs freely | Dyspneic or shallow | Apneic |
| Circulation | Blood pressure within `20 mmHg` of baseline | Within `20-50 mmHg` | More than `50 mmHg` off |
| Consciousness | Fully awake | Rousable on calling | Not responding |
| Oxygen saturation | Over `92%` on room air | Needs oxygen to hold over `90%` | Under `90%` on oxygen |

A score of `9` or more is the common threshold for release from the recovery area.

## What you chart, and how often

During sedation, a full set at least every `5 minutes`: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, end-tidal CO2 and the level of sedation. Every drug with dose, route and exact time. Every airway intervention, however small, with its time. A chin lift is a documented event.

In recovery, at least every `15 minutes` until criteria are met, commonly for about `30 minutes` after the last dose and after the patient is awake.

> **Key:** The riskiest stretch is the five minutes after the procedure ends, when the painful stimulus stops and the room relaxes. That is exactly when peak drug effect can land.

## Capnography patterns worth naming

- **Rising EtCO2 with a falling rate:** hypoventilation, the opioid signature. Stimulate and coach a deep breath, and tell the provider.
- **Low, blunted, irregular waveform:** partial obstruction. Reposition, chin lift, jaw thrust.
- **Flat line:** apnea, or a displaced cannula. Look at the chest first.

## Discharge, item by item

1. Alert and oriented to their own baseline.
2. Vital signs stable and near pre-procedure values.
3. Airway protected, breathing unassisted, saturation at baseline on room air.
4. Pain and nausea controlled.
5. Able to sit and, in most departments, walk without dizziness.
6. Tolerating oral fluid if policy requires it.
7. A responsible adult to drive and to observe them.
8. Written instructions: no driving, machinery, alcohol or legal decisions for `24 hours`.

> **Trap:** "He looks fine" is not a discharge criterion. Residual drug effect outlasts an alert appearance by hours, and the responsible adult requirement is the one that cannot be waived by how well the patient seems.

> **On shift:** Score RASS the same way every time and chart the number. A run of `0`, then `-2`, then `-4` across fifteen minutes is a patient going deeper than planned, and nobody sees it if every person describes it in their own words.
keyPoints: RASS runs +4 to -5 and is scored by observation, then voice, then physical stimulation; ED targets are usually 0 to -2.
Aldrete scores activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness and saturation 0-2 each, and 9 or more is the usual discharge threshold.
Chart a full set every 5 minutes during sedation and every 15 in recovery, including every airway intervention with its time.
The five minutes after the procedure ends are the riskiest, because peak drug effect can arrive once the stimulus stops.
A responsible adult and written 24-hour restrictions are discharge criteria, not courtesies.

checks.q: A sedated patient does not respond to his name but moves when you rub his sternum. What is his RASS score?
checks.why: No response to voice with movement to physical stimulation is deep sedation, RASS -4. A -3 opens the eyes or moves to voice, a -2 wakes briefly to voice, and a -5 does not respond to physical stimulation at all.

checks.q: Which Aldrete item is most often the one keeping a patient in recovery after ED procedural sedation?
choices: Activity: moving all four limbs on command
Consciousness: being fully awake rather than only rousable on calling
Circulation: blood pressure within 20 mmHg of baseline
Oxygen saturation above 92% on room air
checks.why: Sedatives most reliably delay full wakefulness, while limb movement, blood pressure and saturation usually return sooner. The patient who is rousable but not fully awake scores 1 rather than 2 and is the common reason the total sits at 8.

checks.q: During recovery a patient's EtCO2 climbs from 38 to 52 mmHg while the respiratory rate falls from 14 to 7. What is this, and what do you do?
choices: Normal post-procedure breathing; continue monitoring silently
Hypoventilation from residual opioid; stimulate, coach a deep breath and tell the provider
Equipment error; change the sampling line
Metabolic acidosis; prepare for intubation
checks.why: Rising carbon dioxide with a slowing rate is the classic opioid pattern and it precedes apnea. Stimulation and coaching usually correct it, with the provider informed in case naloxone is needed. Metabolic acidosis drives the rate up and the EtCO2 down, the opposite pattern.

lessons.title: The rapid response call, scripted, and handing off a monitored patient
lessons.body:
## The call, word for word

You do not need permission and you do not need to be right. Every rapid response system in the country is built on the arithmetic that a wrong call costs three minutes and a missed one costs a life.

Have these in hand before you dial: room number, the patient's age and reason for visit, the last two sets of vital signs with times, and what changed.

The script, about twenty seconds.

1. **Who and where.** "This is Jose, ED tech, room 8."
2. **The patient.** "Sixty-four-year-old woman, here for abdominal pain since this morning."
3. **The concern, with numbers and a trend.** "Her respiratory rate has gone 18, 22, 28 over forty minutes, systolic dropped from 128 to 88, temperature `38.9 C`, and she is confused now. She was oriented an hour ago."
4. **The ask.** "I need someone at the bedside now."

Then add what is already done: "She is on the monitor, two `18 gauge` IVs, oxygen at `2 L`, and I have not moved her."

> **Trap:** Softeners destroy the call. "When you get a chance", "it might be nothing", "if you are not busy" all convert an emergency into a request that can be queued.

## While you wait, and when they arrive

Do not leave the patient. Get them on the monitor if they are not already, take a full set with a counted respiratory rate, put the head of the bed where the patient breathes best, bring oxygen and suction to the bedside, confirm IV access, clear the doorway and move furniture out of the way, and get the crash cart outside the room.

When the team arrives, give the same four-part story in one pass without editorializing, then take a job: compressions, timekeeping, runner, documentation. Say out loud what you are doing, and say it again when you hand it to someone else.

## Handing off a monitored patient

A monitored patient's handoff carries an extra layer, because what you are transferring is not only a condition but a **watch**.

Use the structure your department recognizes. SBAR is the common one.

- **Situation:** name, age, room, chief complaint, how long they have been here.
- **Background:** relevant history, allergies, what has been done, medications with times.
- **Assessment:** the current numbers and, more importantly, their direction. "Heart rate is 96; it was 78 at noon."
- **Recommendation:** what needs doing and when. "Repeat vitals due at 1515, and she needs that potassium rechecked."

For a monitored patient, add six things explicitly.

1. What the alarm limits are set to, and why, if they were customized.
2. Alarm history and what you fixed. "The V lead kept dropping; I changed the electrodes at 1400."
3. Which numbers have been unreliable and why. "His saturation only reads on the right ear."
4. Who the named watcher is for anyone on continuous observation.
5. Pending results, pending imaging, and what the patient is waiting on.
6. What worries you. This is the part most often left out and the most valuable sentence in the handoff.

## Transport off the unit

A monitored patient going to CT is still a monitored patient. Before they move, confirm who is going, that the transport monitor is charged and working, that the oxygen tank holds enough for the round trip, that suction and a bag-valve-mask travel with anyone whose airway is a question, and that the receiving area knows what is coming.

> **Key:** Hand off the watch, not just the patient. Say the name of the person taking it and get an answer back.

> **On shift:** "And here is what worries me" belongs in every handoff you give. It costs five seconds and it is the only part that transfers judgment rather than data.
keyPoints: The rapid response script is four parts: who and where, the patient, the concern with numbers and a trend, and a direct ask.
Softening phrases turn an emergency into a queued request; state numbers and ask for a person at the bedside.
While waiting: stay with the patient, full set of vitals, monitor, oxygen and suction at the bedside, doorway cleared, cart outside.
A monitored handoff adds alarm limits and history, unreliable readings, the named watcher, pending results, and what worries you.
A monitored patient leaving for imaging needs a named escort, a charged transport monitor and enough oxygen for the round trip.

checks.q: Which rapid response phrasing is correct?
choices: "When you get a chance, could someone take a look at room 8? It might be nothing."

"This is Jose, ED tech, room 8. Sixty-four-year-old with abdominal pain. Respiratory rate 18 to 28 over forty minutes, systolic 128 down to 88, temp 38.9, newly confused. I need someone at the bedside now."
"Room 8 does not look right to me; I have a bad feeling about her."
"Can the doctor swing by room 8 at some point this hour?"
checks.why: The effective call names who and where, the patient, the numbers with their direction, and a direct request for a person at the bedside. The others contain either no data or no ask, which is how urgent patients get deferred behind everything else in the queue.

checks.q: You are handing off a monitored patient at shift change. Which item is most often omitted and most valuable?
choices: The patient's date of birth
The exact model of monitor in use
What worries you about this patient
The time the patient arrived
checks.why: Identifiers and arrival times are already in the record, and the equipment model is irrelevant. Concern is the only element that transfers judgment rather than data, and it is the part people feel awkward saying and therefore skip.

checks.q: A monitored patient on continuous observation needs a CT. What must happen before transport?
choices: The monitor is removed and reapplied on return to save battery
A named person goes with the patient, with a charged transport monitor, enough oxygen for the round trip, and suction and a bag-valve-mask if the airway is a question
The receiving area is told afterward, once the patient arrives
Telemetry is simply left running and checked when the signal returns
checks.why: Transport is the period where monitored patients most often become unmonitored. Ownership has to be explicit, the equipment has to be verified before leaving, and the receiving area needs to know what is coming. Leaving telemetry running out of range monitors nobody.

cards.front: What is the first move on any alarm?
cards.back: Look at the patient, then look at the screen. A talking patient under a flat trace is a lead problem; a grey patient under a perfect trace is a patient problem.

cards.front: What three questions do you ask after an alarm sounds?
cards.back: Does the waveform match the number? Is there a mechanical cause I can fix in thirty seconds? If not, escalate with parameter, value, trend, patient and room.

cards.front: The monitor alarms asystole and the patient is eating lunch. What is happening?
cards.back: An electrode is off. Replace it and re-prep the skin. Never silence from the desk, and never widen a limit to quiet a mechanical problem.

cards.front: How do you tell a real SpO2 of 88% from a probe problem?
cards.back: The pleth waveform and the patient. A clean pleth with accessory muscle use and short sentences is real. A flat ragged pleth on a warm, talking patient is the probe.

cards.front: Which three alarms are treated as real before anything else?
cards.back: A new wide-complex tachycardia in a patient who looks unwell, any alarm on a patient not answering you, and a capnography alarm on a sedated or intubated patient.

cards.front: Blood pressure alarms at 70/40 on a grey, cool, sleepy patient. What do you do?
cards.back: Escalate immediately, then confirm manually while help is coming. Repeating cycles first costs minutes on a patient who already matches the number.

cards.front: What is the difference between silencing, adjusting and hiding an alarm?
cards.back: Silencing follows going to the bedside and finding the cause. Adjusting changes a limit that is genuinely wrong for the patient, by the nurse or per protocol. Widening a limit to stop a mechanical alarm is hiding.

cards.front: Name the fixable causes behind most false alarms.
cards.back: Dried-out electrodes, unprepped skin, cables under tension, a cuff a size too small, and a probe on a cold hand.

cards.front: Why does fixing a false alarm at the source count as clinical work?
cards.back: Every unfixed false alarm makes the next real one less likely to be answered. Alarm fatigue has killed patients, so removing noise protects the next alarm.

cards.front: Where do the three-lead electrodes go?
cards.back: White on the right upper chest, black on the left upper chest, red on the left lower chest or abdomen. White on right, smoke over fire.

cards.front: What do the green and brown electrodes do on a five-lead system?
cards.back: Green is the ground, on the right lower chest or abdomen. Brown is the single chest lead, usually placed at V1: fourth intercostal space just right of the sternum.

cards.front: Why is lead II the default monitoring view?
cards.back: It runs roughly parallel to the heart's normal electrical axis, so complexes are tall and upright, P waves are clearest, and rate counting is most reliable.

cards.front: List the skin prep steps for reliable electrodes.
cards.back: Dry the skin, wipe off oils with alcohol and let it dry or use the abrasive tab, clip rather than shave hair, check the gel is moist, and leave slack in the cable.

cards.front: How often are monitoring electrodes changed?
cards.back: At least every 24 hours, and after defibrillation, heavy sweating or a shower. A dried-out electrode looks fine and works badly.

cards.front: What causes a fine fuzzy baseline versus a slow rolling baseline?
cards.back: Fine rapid fuzz is muscle tremor, shivering or anxiety. Slow rolling drift is a loose electrode, respiration or patient movement.

cards.front: What single check resolves most artifact questions?
cards.back: Feel a pulse while watching the screen. If the rate you feel and the rate displayed disagree, the screen is wrong.

cards.front: What causes a monitor to double count the heart rate?
cards.back: A tall T wave or a pacer spike counted as a second beat. Change the lead the monitor counts from or adjust gain per policy, and tell the nurse.

cards.front: What does lost telemetry on a monitored patient mean?
cards.back: That nobody is watching. It is reported, not waited out, and a patient leaving the unit needs a named escort with a working transport monitor.

cards.front: What does a capnogram baseline above zero indicate?
cards.back: Rebreathing of exhaled carbon dioxide: an exhausted absorber, a faulty valve, or insufficient fresh gas flow.

cards.front: What does an upsloping plateau on a capnogram mean?
cards.back: Uneven alveolar emptying from obstruction, classically bronchospasm in asthma or COPD. Combined with a slurred upstroke it makes the shark fin shape.

cards.front: What is a curare cleft?
cards.back: A notch dipping down in the middle of the plateau, caused by a paralyzed patient starting to breathe as neuromuscular blockade wears off.

cards.front: How does EtCO2 change as an asthma attack worsens?
cards.back: It starts low, often 25-30 mmHg, from hyperventilation. As the patient tires it rises toward and past normal. A normal value in a still-struggling asthmatic is a danger sign.

cards.front: Why is a squaring-off shark fin useful during a breathing treatment?
cards.back: The shape improves before the patient reports feeling better, so it is objective evidence the bronchodilator is working. A fin that stays rounded through three treatments is a non-responder.

cards.front: Name the three sedation capnography patterns in order of severity.
cards.back: Rising EtCO2 with a slowing rate is hypoventilation. A low blunted irregular waveform is partial obstruction. A flat line is apnea or a displaced cannula.

cards.front: A ventilated patient's EtCO2 drops suddenly with an intact circuit and a normal waveform shape. What does it mean?
cards.back: Blood is not reaching the lungs. Massive pulmonary embolism or a sudden loss of cardiac output until proven otherwise.

cards.front: What does a low EtCO2 with a fast rate and clear lungs suggest?
cards.back: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis: diabetic ketoacidosis, sepsis with high lactate, salicylate toxicity, or severe kidney failure.

cards.front: What three questions does EtCO2 answer at once?
cards.back: Is air moving (ventilation), is blood moving (circulation), and is metabolism normal. Which one it is answering depends on the rest of the patient.

cards.front: When does the sepsis clock usually start?
cards.back: At triage, when the first concerning set of numbers is recorded, not at the physician's diagnosis. That is why an honest first set of vitals matters so much.

cards.front: List the five items of the hour-1 sepsis bundle.
cards.back: Measure lactate, draw blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or higher, and add vasopressors if MAP stays under 65.

cards.front: How much fluid is 30 mL/kg in an 80 kg adult, and how does it run?
cards.back: 2400 mL, through large-bore access under a pressure bag or rapid infuser. Gravity through a small catheter cannot deliver it in the time the bundle intends.

cards.front: Why does a repeat lactate matter?
cards.back: Clearance is the response marker. A lactate falling from 4.2 to 2.6 means the patient is responding; one that rises means they are not. Repeat if the first was over 2 mmol/L.

cards.front: What mean arterial pressure and urine output are targeted in sepsis?
cards.back: MAP at least 65 mmHg and urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/h, roughly 30 mL/h in an average adult, measured and reported hourly.

cards.front: What is source control, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Physically removing or draining the infection: an abscess drained, an infected line pulled, an obstructed kidney decompressed, dead bowel resected. Antibiotics do not work around an undrained source.

cards.front: What is the most commonly missed item in a sepsis handoff?
cards.back: How much of the 30 mL/kg actually infused. A bag hung is not a bag infused, and the next team plans from that number.

cards.front: A septic patient goes quiet and stops complaining while the heart rate rises. What is happening?
cards.back: Deterioration, not improvement. Falling agitation with a rising heart rate is a brain running out of perfusion.

cards.front: What are the three GCS components and their ranges?
cards.back: Eye opening 1-4, verbal 1-5, motor 1-6, totalling 3-15. An intubated patient's verbal score is reported as 1T or not testable.

cards.front: What is the difference between GCS motor 5 and motor 4?
cards.back: Motor 5 localizes: the patient reaches toward the stimulus and tries to remove it. Motor 4 only withdraws. The difference reflects cortical function.

cards.front: Why must painful stimulus for GCS be applied centrally?
cards.back: A spinal reflex can move a limb with no brain involvement, so a peripheral stimulus can overscore. Use a trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure, and score the best response.

cards.front: What three things are recorded for each pupil?
cards.back: Size in millimetres, shape, and reaction as brisk, sluggish or none. Then check the consensual response: light in one eye should constrict both.

cards.front: What does a new unilateral dilated sluggish pupil mean?
cards.back: Third nerve compression from rising pressure on that side. It is an emergency and is reported the moment it is seen, not at the end of the round.

cards.front: What do bilateral pinpoint reactive pupils suggest?
cards.back: Opioid effect, or a pontine lesion. Compare with bilateral mid-position fixed pupils, which suggest midbrain injury.

cards.front: What does the NIHSS measure, and what is its range?
cards.back: Eleven items covering consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, arm and leg strength, ataxia, sensation, language, speech clarity and neglect. Total 0-42, with higher meaning worse.

cards.front: Which single piece of stroke history matters most?
cards.back: Time of last known well, because it determines eligibility for thrombolysis and thrombectomy. Confirm it with family directly rather than accepting a vague estimate.

cards.front: What GCS change is reported immediately?
cards.back: A drop of 2 or more points, or any new pupil asymmetry. Report components and times, not adjectives: E2 V2 M4 at 0910, was E3 V4 M6 at 0855.

cards.front: Why do most deteriorating patients not trigger an alarm?
cards.back: Because deterioration shows first as a trend, a physical sign or a behavior change, and all of those can occur while every value is still inside the alarm limits.

cards.front: Which two deterioration patterns look like improvement?
cards.back: The asthmatic whose chest goes quiet, and the acutely ill patient who suddenly settles and wants to sleep. Both are commonly charted as resting comfortably.

cards.front: What does a narrowing pulse pressure indicate?
cards.back: Vasoconstriction defending a falling volume. Pressures running 128/72, then 118/80, then 106/88 show a patient compensating for volume loss even though the systolic is still acceptable.

cards.front: Calculate and interpret the shock index for a heart rate of 110 and a systolic of 108.
cards.back: 110 divided by 108 is about 1.0. Normal is 0.5-0.7, and over 0.9 predicts serious illness and transfusion need. Both numbers look acceptable alone.

cards.front: What does spreading mottling over the knees signify?
cards.back: Peripheral shutdown from severe shock, often before the blood pressure falls. Mottling that spreads outward from the knee is a marker of poor outcome.

cards.front: What three habits catch deterioration the monitor misses?
cards.back: Compare with the previous set before charting, touch the patient every round for skin temperature and capillary refill, and ask one question that requires thought rather than a yes or no.

cards.front: Why is a patient in alcohol withdrawal who begins hallucinating urgent?
cards.back: Escalating withdrawal heads toward delirium tremens, which carries real mortality. A rising heart rate, tremor, sweating and hallucinations together need treatment now, not observation.

cards.front: Why check a sickle cell patient before letting her sleep after opioids?
cards.back: Withdrawal into sleep during acute illness can be a falling level of consciousness, and opioids depress breathing. Count the rate and check capnography first.

cards.front: What are the three sides of the pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.back: Appearance (tone, interactivity, consolability, gaze, cry), work of breathing, and circulation to the skin. Any one abnormal means a sick child; all three means a resuscitation.

cards.front: What is the formula for pediatric hypotension?
cards.back: Systolic below 70 plus twice the age in years, for ages 1-10. Below 90 from age 10 up, below 70 for infants, below 60 for neonates.

cards.front: Why is bradycardia in a child an emergency?
cards.back: It is hypoxia until proven otherwise. Children compensate with tachycardia until oxygen runs out, so a falling rate is the step immediately before arrest.

cards.front: What does grunting in an infant mean?
cards.back: The child is closing the glottis against exhalation to generate their own positive pressure. It is a sign of severe respiratory distress, not a minor noise.

cards.front: What distinguishes mild from escalating croup?
cards.back: Stridor only with crying is milder; stridor at rest is the escalation. Keep the child calm on a parent's lap, because agitation worsens the obstruction.

cards.front: Where do you check capillary refill in a child?
cards.back: Centrally, at the chest or the kneecap. A cold hand or foot gives a falsely prolonged result and a falsely alarming picture.

cards.front: Where does the SpO2 probe go on an infant?
cards.back: On a toe, a foot, or a wrapped hand. Motion is the main enemy, so a settled child on a parent's chest gives a better trace than a fighting child on a stretcher.

cards.front: Why is a normal heart rate in a very ill-looking child not reassuring?
cards.back: It may be the brief passage between compensatory tachycardia and pre-arrest bradycardia. Appearance and perfusion outrank a single reassuring number.

cards.front: Why is comfort a measurement technique in pediatrics?
cards.back: An upset child produces motion artifact on the pleth, a fictional impedance respiratory rate, and a blood pressure taken mid-scream. A settled child produces data worth charting.

cards.front: How is RASS scored, step by step?
cards.back: Observe for 10 seconds. If not alert, say the name and ask for eye contact. If still nothing, shake the shoulder, then rub the sternum. The level at which they respond is the score.

cards.front: What RASS score is no response to voice but movement to physical stimulation?
cards.back: Minus 4, deep sedation. Minus 5 has no response even to physical stimulation, and minus 3 opens the eyes or moves to voice without eye contact.

cards.front: What RASS range is targeted for most sedated ED patients?
cards.back: Zero to minus 2: drowsy but rousable. Deeper sedation prolongs ventilation and worsens outcomes without adding benefit.

cards.front: Name the five Aldrete items.
cards.back: Activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness and oxygen saturation, each scored 0-2 for a total out of 10. Nine or more is the common discharge threshold.

cards.front: How does Aldrete score circulation?
cards.back: 2 points for blood pressure within 20 mmHg of the pre-procedure value, 1 point for 20-50 mmHg off, and 0 for more than 50 mmHg off.

cards.front: What are the documentation intervals during and after sedation?
cards.back: A full set including EtCO2 and sedation level at least every 5 minutes during, and at least every 15 minutes in recovery until criteria are met, typically about 30 minutes after the last dose.

cards.front: Why is the period right after a procedure ends the riskiest?
cards.back: The painful stimulus that was keeping the patient aroused disappears just as peak drug effect can arrive, and the room relaxes at the same moment.

cards.front: Which discharge criterion cannot be waived by how well a patient looks?
cards.back: A responsible adult to drive and observe, with written 24-hour restrictions on driving, machinery, alcohol and legal decisions. Residual drug effect outlasts an alert appearance.

cards.front: Give the four parts of a rapid response call.
cards.back: Who and where, the patient in one line, the concern with numbers and their trend, and a direct ask for someone at the bedside now.

cards.front: Which phrases weaken a rapid response call?
cards.back: When you get a chance, if you are not busy, it might be nothing, does not look right to me. Softeners convert an emergency into a queued request.

cards.front: What do you do while waiting for the rapid response team?
cards.back: Stay with the patient, monitor on, full set with a counted respiratory rate, head of bed positioned for breathing, oxygen and suction at the bedside, IV confirmed, doorway cleared, crash cart outside.

cards.front: What does SBAR stand for and contain?
cards.back: Situation (who, where, why here), Background (history, allergies, what has been done), Assessment (current numbers and their direction), Recommendation (what needs doing and when).

cards.front: What six extra items belong in a monitored patient's handoff?
cards.back: Alarm limits and why, alarm history and what you fixed, which readings are unreliable and why, the named watcher, pending results, and what worries you.

cards.front: What must be confirmed before a monitored patient leaves for imaging?
cards.back: Who is going, a charged working transport monitor, enough oxygen for the round trip, suction and a bag-valve-mask if the airway is a question, and that the receiving area is expecting them.

cards.front: What does handing off the watch mean?
cards.back: Naming the person taking responsibility for a continuously observed patient out loud and getting an answer back. Assuming someone is watching is how patients are found down.

quiz.q: A ventricular tachycardia alarm sounds. You walk in and the patient is sitting up brushing her teeth, and the spikes on the trace match the rhythm of her brushing. What do you do?
choices: Confirm she is well, stop the motion, verify the rhythm in a second lead, and then silence at the bedside
Call a code and prepare the defibrillator
Silence the alarm from the central station and continue your round
Widen the high heart rate limit so it stops triggering
quiz.why: Rhythmic motion artifact reproduces ventricular tachycardia exactly, and a comfortable patient brushing her teeth is not in VT. Confirming in a second lead proves it. Calling a code wastes a team, and silencing without looking or widening limits hides the finding.

quiz.q: The monitor alarms SpO2 82%. The pleth waveform is flat and ragged, the patient's hands are cold, and he is speaking in full sentences. What is the first step?
choices: Apply a non-rebreather mask at 15 L
Call a rapid response
Warm the hand, move the probe to another finger or the ear, and recheck
Chart the value and continue monitoring
quiz.why: A flat ragged pleth means the probe is not detecting arterial pulsation, so the number is not a measurement. Full sentences argue against real hypoxemia. Treating or escalating on an invalid number wastes resources, and charting it without a note propagates the error.

quiz.q: Which action is appropriate when an alarm limit is genuinely wrong for a specific patient?
choices: Silence the alarm each time it sounds
Have the nurse adjust the limit to the patient's real physiology, per protocol, and document it
Turn the alarm volume to zero for that bed
Disable the parameter entirely
quiz.why: Adjusting is a deliberate, documented change made by the nurse or under protocol for real physiology, such as a COPD patient who lives at 88 percent. Repeated silencing, zero volume and disabling all leave the patient effectively unmonitored and are never acceptable.

quiz.q: You are assigned to six monitored patients and the same asystole alarm has triggered four times in an hour on one of them, each time a lead artifact. What is the correct response the fourth time?
choices: Assume artifact again and silence it remotely
Widen the low heart rate limit to prevent further alarms
Turn the bed's alarm volume down so it stops distracting the team
Go to the bedside again, and fix the root cause by re-prepping the skin and replacing the electrodes
quiz.why: Repeated false alarms are a problem to solve, not a pattern to trust, because the fifth one may be real. Fixing the electrodes at the source removes the noise permanently. Every other option makes the next genuine alarm less likely to be answered.

quiz.q: A sedated patient's capnography alarm sounds. Which assumption should you start with?
choices: The sampling line has been dislodged
The monitor needs recalibration
That the patient is apneic or the airway is obstructed, until you have looked at the chest
That the alarm limit is set too tightly
quiz.why: On a sedated patient a capnography alarm is treated as real first, because apnea is the one thing that kills within minutes. Equipment causes are common but are checked after you have confirmed the chest is moving, not before.

quiz.q: Which statement about silencing an alarm is correct?
choices: Silencing is acceptable from the central station when the patient was fine ten minutes ago
Silencing is appropriate only after going to the bedside, seeing the patient, and identifying the cause
Silencing should be avoided entirely in every situation
Silencing and adjusting the limit are the same action
quiz.why: Silencing is legitimate once you have laid eyes on the patient and know why the alarm fired. Doing it from the desk is a clinical judgment about someone unseen. It is not forbidden, and it is different from adjusting a limit, which changes future alarm behavior.

quiz.q: You are placing a five-lead monitor. Where does the green electrode go?
choices: Right lower chest or abdomen, as the ground
Left upper chest
Fourth intercostal space right of the sternum
Left mid-axillary line
quiz.why: Green is the ground electrode and sits on the right lower chest or abdomen, opposite the red on the left. The left upper chest is black, V1 is the brown chest lead, and the left mid-axillary line is a defibrillation pad position.

quiz.q: A patient's ECG trace has a slow rolling baseline that drifts up and down with each breath, making rhythm interpretation difficult. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Electrical interference from a nearby infusion pump
Muscle tremor
Double counting of the T wave
A loose electrode combined with chest movement
quiz.why: Slow rolling drift is a contact problem, usually an electrode lifting with respiration or movement, and the fix is re-prepping and reattaching. Interference produces regular fast spikes, tremor produces fine fuzz, and double counting changes the rate rather than the baseline.

quiz.q: A diaphoretic patient's electrodes keep falling off during a busy resuscitation. What is the correct fix?
choices: Tape the existing electrodes down over the sweat
Dry the skin thoroughly, wipe with alcohol and let it dry, then apply fresh electrodes with slack in the cables
Shave the chest with a razor to improve adhesion
Switch to pulse oximetry alone for rhythm monitoring
