quiz.why: Sweat breaks the electrical contact, so fresh electrodes on genuinely dry, degreased skin are the answer. Taping over sweat preserves the bad contact, a razor causes micro-cuts and infection risk where clipping would do, and oximetry cannot show rhythm.

quiz.q: A monitor reports a heart rate of 44 on a patient whose radial pulse you count at 88. The complexes on screen look very small. What is the likely explanation?
choices: The patient has a pulse deficit from atrial fibrillation
The monitor is double counting
Low-voltage complexes are being undercounted, so the displayed rate is lower than the true rate
The SpO2 probe is on the same arm as the cuff
quiz.why: Small complexes from obesity, emphysema or a pericardial effusion can fall below the counting threshold, halving the displayed rate. A pulse deficit gives a palpated rate lower than the monitor, not higher, and double counting produces the opposite error.

quiz.q: Why is lead II chosen as the default monitoring lead rather than lead III?
choices: It runs closest to the heart's normal electrical axis, giving the tallest clearest complexes and the most reliable rate counting
It is the only lead that detects ST elevation
It requires fewer electrodes
It is least affected by electrical interference
quiz.why: Alignment with the normal axis makes P waves and R waves tall and upright, which is what both the human eye and the counting algorithm need. All limb leads use the same electrodes, no single monitoring lead is a substitute for a 12-lead for ST changes, and interference affects all leads alike.

quiz.q: A capnogram shows a slurred upstroke that slopes continuously into an upsloping plateau, with an EtCO2 of 28 mmHg in a patient working hard to breathe. What does this picture represent?
choices: Rebreathing of exhaled gas
Esophageal intubation
Bronchospasm with hyperventilation, as in an acute asthma attack
Massive pulmonary embolism
quiz.why: The shark fin shape is uneven alveolar emptying from obstruction, and the low value reflects hyperventilation early in the attack. Rebreathing raises the baseline, esophageal placement gives no sustained waveform, and pulmonary embolism drops the value without slurring the shape.

quiz.q: A severe asthmatic has been treated for 40 minutes. His EtCO2 has risen from 26 to 44 mmHg, he is still using accessory muscles, and he has become quiet. What is the interpretation?
choices: He is improving, since the EtCO2 is now normal
He is tiring and heading toward respiratory failure
He has developed a pneumothorax
The capnography sampling line is partially blocked
quiz.why: Early asthma drives the value down by hyperventilation, so a return to normal while the patient still struggles means the compensating ventilation is failing. Becoming quiet adds a second danger sign. A blocked line would distort the waveform rather than produce a smooth rise.

quiz.q: A capnogram baseline sits at 6 mmHg instead of returning to zero between breaths. What does this indicate?
choices: A leak in the circuit
Bronchospasm
Cardiac arrest
Rebreathing of exhaled carbon dioxide
quiz.why: A baseline above zero means carbon dioxide is present at the start of inspiration, which happens when exhaled gas is being re-inhaled: an exhausted absorber, a faulty valve or insufficient fresh gas flow. Bronchospasm changes the upstroke and plateau, and arrest flattens the trace entirely.

quiz.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing 34 times a minute with clear lungs and an EtCO2 of 17 mmHg. What does this represent?
choices: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis
Impending respiratory arrest
A massive pulmonary embolism
Hyperventilation from anxiety alone
quiz.why: Deep rapid breathing blows off carbon dioxide deliberately to offset the acid load, which is Kussmaul respiration. It is hard work, and a rise back toward normal would mean the compensation is failing. Embolism drops EtCO2 through poor perfusion rather than through a very high respiratory rate with clear lungs.

quiz.q: During procedural sedation the EtCO2 rises from 36 to 51 mmHg while the respiratory rate falls from 16 to 8. The saturation is 97% on 2 L. What is happening and what comes first?
choices: Normal sedation; continue observing
Airway obstruction; apply suction immediately
Opioid-related hypoventilation; stimulate the patient, coach a deep breath, and tell the provider
Equipment failure; replace the sampling cannula
quiz.why: Rising carbon dioxide with a falling rate is the classic opioid pattern and is the warning before apnea. Stimulation and coaching usually correct it. Obstruction blunts and distorts the waveform rather than producing a smooth rise, and the saturation is not yet useful information.

quiz.q: A paralyzed, ventilated patient's capnogram develops a small downward notch in the middle of the plateau. What does this mean?
choices: A cuff leak around the endotracheal tube
The neuromuscular blockade is wearing off and the patient is starting to breathe
The patient has developed bronchospasm
The ventilator rate is set too high
quiz.why: That notch is a curare cleft, made by the patient's own inspiratory effort interrupting the machine breath, so it signals returning respiratory drive and prompts reassessment of sedation and paralysis. A leak affects the plateau height and downstroke, and bronchospasm slurs the upstroke.

quiz.q: A 70 kg patient with septic shock needs 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. What volume is required?
choices: 700 mL
quiz.why: 30 mL/kg times 70 kg is 2100 mL. The other options correspond to 10, 20 and 25 mL/kg, and under-resuscitating a septic patient because of arithmetic is a real and avoidable failure.

quiz.q: A patient with suspected sepsis has a blood pressure of 84/50 after the full fluid bolus, giving a mean arterial pressure of 61 mmHg. What does the bundle call for next?
choices: A vasopressor to bring the mean arterial pressure to at least 65 mmHg
A second 30 mL/kg bolus regardless of response
Repeating the blood pressure in one hour
Discontinuing antibiotics until cultures result
quiz.why: A mean under 65 despite adequate fluid is the trigger for vasopressors, most often norepinephrine. Automatically repeating the full bolus risks fluid overload, waiting an hour loses time, and antibiotics are never held pending cultures once they have been given.

quiz.q: A septic patient's initial lactate was 4.6 mmol/L. Three hours later it is 5.8 mmol/L despite fluids and antibiotics. What does this mean?
choices: The laboratory result is likely spurious
Lactate always rises for the first six hours of treatment
The patient is not responding, and the team needs to know immediately
Lactate clearance is not a useful marker in sepsis
quiz.why: Falling lactate marks response, so a rising value means tissue oxygen debt is worsening and the plan needs to change, often with vasopressors or source control. Clearance is one of the standard reassessment markers, and a rise is not an expected part of successful treatment.

quiz.q: Which route of temperature measurement is most appropriate in a shocked, peripherally cold septic patient whose oral reading is 36.2 C?
choices: Repeat the oral reading after the patient closes their mouth longer
A core route such as rectal, because peripheral and oral readings underestimate temperature in a vasoconstricted patient
Axillary, which is the most reliable in adults
Temporal artery scan, which is unaffected by perfusion
quiz.why: Shunting of blood away from the periphery and mouth makes surface and oral readings read low, which can hide fever or hypothermia and delay a sepsis alert. Axillary and temporal methods are also perfusion-dependent and are less reliable, not more.

quiz.q: Antibiotics are hanging, a liter of fluid is running, and it is now 2 hours since the sepsis clock started. Which reassessment item is most often skipped?
choices: Rechecking the temperature
Documenting the allergy list
Confirming the patient's ride home
Repeating the lactate, measuring hourly urine output, and reassessing perfusion by hand
quiz.why: The reassessment block at one to three hours is the part of the bundle most often left undone, yet lactate clearance, urine output and physical perfusion signs are what tell you whether the treatment is working. The other items are routine but do not answer that question.

quiz.q: Why does the sepsis clock usually start at triage rather than at the physician's diagnosis?
choices: Because the earliest recorded abnormal vital signs define when the patient could first have been identified, and mortality tracks from that point
Because triage nurses order the antibiotics
Because billing requires a triage timestamp
Because the physician's note is written later in the visit
quiz.why: The clock reflects when recognition was possible, which is why an accurate first set of vital signs is so consequential. Antibiotics are ordered by a provider, and the timing convention exists for outcome reasons rather than administrative ones.

quiz.q: A head injury patient opens his eyes only when you pinch his trapezius, makes incomprehensible groaning sounds, and pulls his arm away from the stimulus without reaching toward it. What is his GCS?
choices: E3 V3 M5, total 11
E2 V2 M4, total 8
E2 V3 M5, total 10
E1 V2 M4, total 7
quiz.why: Eye opening to pain is E2, incomprehensible sounds are V2, and withdrawal without reaching toward the stimulus is M4, totalling 8, which is the threshold at which the airway is considered unprotected. Reaching toward the stimulus would be M5 and a higher total.

quiz.q: Which pupil finding is most urgent?
choices: Both pupils 2 mm and briskly reactive in a patient who received morphine
Pupils 3 mm and 4 mm, both briskly reactive, in an alert patient who says they have always been that way
A right pupil that was 3 mm and brisk an hour ago and is now 6 mm and sluggish
Both pupils 4 mm and briskly reactive after an eye examination
quiz.why: A pupil that has changed since the last documented check suggests third nerve compression from rising intracranial pressure and is an emergency. Opioid miosis, longstanding physiologic anisocoria with brisk reactions, and post-examination findings are all explainable and stable.

quiz.q: Why is a trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure preferred over a nail bed stimulus when scoring GCS motor response?
choices: A central stimulus tests brain-mediated response, while a peripheral one can trigger a spinal reflex that overstates function
A central stimulus hurts less
Nail bed pressure is prohibited by policy
Peripheral stimuli cannot be applied to intubated patients
quiz.why: Limb withdrawal from a peripheral stimulus can occur through a spinal reflex arc even with severe brain injury, which inflates the motor score. Central stimuli require brain processing. The choice is about validity, not comfort or policy.

quiz.q: A stroke patient is 45 minutes past thrombolytic administration. Blood pressure reads 196/112. What does this require?
choices: Rechecking in 30 minutes as scheduled
Nothing, since hypertension is expected after a stroke
Encouraging the patient to relax and rechecking
Immediate notification, because blood pressure is held under roughly 180/105 after thrombolytics to reduce the risk of bleeding into the brain
quiz.why: Thrombolytics plus uncontrolled hypertension is the combination that produces intracranial hemorrhage, so the ceiling is enforced actively with treatment rather than observed. Waiting for the next scheduled check or attributing it to stress loses the window to intervene.

quiz.q: Which is the most useful way to report a neurological change?
choices: "He is not doing as well as before"
"E2 V2 M4 at 0910, was E3 V4 M6 at 0855, and his right pupil is now 6 mm and sluggish"
"His GCS dropped"
"He seems more sedated than earlier"
quiz.why: Components, values and times let another clinician act without re-examining from scratch and make the size and speed of the change obvious. Adjectives and a bare statement that the score dropped leave the listener needing to start over.

quiz.q: A family member says the stroke patient was 'fine at dinner last night' and was found with weakness this morning. Why does this matter so much?
choices: It determines whether the patient can eat
It establishes the NIHSS score
Last known well determines eligibility for thrombolysis and thrombectomy, so it is the most consequential piece of history in the room
It determines which nurse is assigned
quiz.why: Treatment windows are measured from last known well, not from symptom discovery, so a patient found in the morning may be outside the window despite waking with symptoms. The NIHSS is scored by examination, and the other options are unrelated.

quiz.q: Over four rechecks a patient's blood pressure reads 128/72, 122/78, 112/82, then 104/88. Heart rate rises from 84 to 108. Every value is inside the alarm limits. What is happening?
choices: Compensated shock: the pulse pressure is narrowing as the patient vasoconstricts to defend a falling volume
Normal variation between automated cycles
Improving pain control
An incorrectly sized cuff
quiz.why: A systolic falling while the diastolic rises is a narrowing pulse pressure, which is the fingerprint of vasoconstriction in response to volume loss, and a rising heart rate confirms it. Random variation does not move both numbers in opposite directions across four readings in a consistent direction.

quiz.q: An 81-year-old admitted for a hip fracture has been pleasant and oriented all morning. At 1400 he cannot tell you the month and keeps asking where his wife is. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Expected sundowning in an elderly inpatient
Fatigue after a long wait in the department
A reaction to the hospital environment that will settle
New confusion, which is a vital sign and is reported as a change with the baseline attached
quiz.why: Acute change in mental status reflects the brain's sensitivity to perfusion, oxygenation, infection and drugs, and it frequently precedes any monitor change. Labelling it as sundowning or fatigue is how hypoxia, sepsis and hypoglycemia get missed in older patients.

quiz.q: Which of these findings requires you to act before any monitor alarms?
choices: A heart rate of 96 in a patient whose baseline is 92
Mottling spreading up from the knees with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a systolic of 104
A single blood pressure reading of 138/84
A respiratory rate of 18 counted accurately
quiz.why: Peripheral shutdown appears before the blood pressure falls and spreading mottling is a marker of severe shock and poor outcome. The other findings are within normal limits or trivially changed from baseline and would not warrant escalation on their own.

quiz.q: A patient with a sickle cell pain crisis received opioids 20 minutes ago and now asks to be left alone to sleep. What do you do before leaving the room?
choices: Dim the lights and let her rest, since pain control is the goal
Wake her every five minutes to prevent sedation
Count her respiratory rate and check the capnography before accepting that she is simply comfortable
Remove the monitor so the alarms do not disturb her
quiz.why: Opioid-induced respiratory depression and a falling level of consciousness both look like a patient settling down. Counting the rate and looking at the waveform separates comfort from sedation. Repeated waking is not monitoring, and removing the monitor is the opposite of what the situation calls for.

quiz.q: Which pair of findings is most often charted as improvement when it actually represents deterioration?
choices: Rising blood pressure and falling heart rate after fluids
Improving oxygen saturation and decreasing respiratory rate after oxygen
Decreasing pain score and increasing urine output
A quiet chest in an asthmatic, and an acutely ill patient who suddenly settles and wants to sleep
quiz.why: Wheeze requires airflow, so its disappearance in a worsening asthmatic means air is no longer moving, and sudden settling in acute illness is often a falling level of consciousness. The other pairs describe genuine response to treatment.

quiz.q: What is the lower limit of normal systolic blood pressure for a 6-year-old?
choices: 82 mmHg
70 mmHg
90 mmHg
100 mmHg
quiz.why: The formula for ages 1 to 10 is 70 plus twice the age in years, giving 82 for a 6-year-old. The flat value of 70 applies to infants, 90 applies from age 10 up, and 100 is an adult-oriented figure that would wrongly label a healthy child as hypotensive.

quiz.q: A 6-month-old with bronchiolitis is breathing 70 times a minute with audible grunting and head bobbing. What does the grunting tell you?
choices: He is congested and needs suctioning only
He is generating his own positive end-expiratory pressure against a closed glottis, which marks severe respiratory distress
He is hungry
He is comfortable and self-soothing
quiz.why: Grunting is an involuntary attempt to keep alveoli open by exhaling against a partly closed glottis, and it is one of the most reliable markers of severe distress in an infant. Treating it as congestion or comfort is how these babies are left unattended.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old with gastroenteritis has a heart rate of 172, capillary refill of 3 seconds at the chest, is alert, and has a blood pressure of 94/58. How should this be reported?
choices: As normal, since the blood pressure is fine for age
As mild dehydration requiring oral fluids only
As compensated shock: tachycardia and delayed refill with a normal pressure, which needs to be escalated now
As anxiety related to the hospital environment
quiz.why: Children defend blood pressure by vasoconstricting and raising heart rate until the compensation abruptly fails, so a normal pressure is reassurance about nothing. Delayed central refill plus marked tachycardia is shock and needs a clinician now.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old has just stopped seizing. He is snoring loudly and the SpO2 reads 88%. What is the first action?
choices: Prepare a second dose of anticonvulsant
Obtain a fingerstick glucose
Place a nasal cannula at 2 L and recheck in five minutes
Reposition the airway with a head tilt or jaw thrust, suction if needed, and apply oxygen while staying at the bedside
quiz.why: Snoring is partial upper airway obstruction from the tongue and soft tissue in the post-ictal state, and repositioning fixes it immediately. Glucose and further medication matter but come after the airway, and low-flow oxygen through an obstructed airway does not reach the lungs.

quiz.q: Why does an adult-sized blood pressure cuff on a small child's arm create a safety risk?
choices: An oversized cuff reads falsely low, which can hide hypotension in a child who is already compensating
An oversized cuff reads falsely high, which triggers unnecessary workups
It cannot inflate properly and will error out every time
It is uncomfortable but produces accurate readings
quiz.why: A cuff too large for the limb requires less pressure to occlude the artery and therefore underestimates the true pressure. In a child, where hypotension is already a late sign, a falsely low reading that looks acceptable removes the last warning there is.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with croup has stridor only when he cries. What is the correct approach?
choices: Lay him flat and inspect the throat with a tongue depressor
Keep him calm on a parent's lap, minimize handling, and watch for the development of stridor at rest
Separate him from the parent so he can be properly monitored
Discharge him to the waiting room as a mild case
quiz.why: Agitation increases turbulent airflow through a narrowed airway and worsens obstruction, so calm is treatment. Stridor at rest marks escalation and is what you watch for. Throat instrumentation in a stridorous child risks precipitating complete obstruction.

quiz.q: A sedated patient opens his eyes and looks at you when you call his name, then loses eye contact after about five seconds. What is his RASS?
quiz.why: Eye opening to voice with eye contact lasting less than 10 seconds is light sedation, RASS -2. A -1 sustains eye contact longer than 10 seconds, 0 is alert and calm, and -4 does not respond to voice at all.

quiz.q: A patient in recovery moves all four limbs on command, breathes deeply and coughs, has a blood pressure 30 mmHg below her pre-procedure value, is rousable only when called, and maintains 95% on room air. What is her Aldrete score?
quiz.why: Activity 2, respiration 2, circulation 1 because the pressure is 20 to 50 mmHg off, consciousness 1 because she is rousable rather than fully awake, and saturation 2, giving 8. The usual threshold is 9, so she stays in recovery.

quiz.q: Why is a chin lift during procedural sedation a documented event?
choices: Because any airway intervention, however small, records that the patient's airway was not self-maintained at that moment, which changes how the sedation is interpreted and reported
Because it is a billable procedure
Because it requires a physician order
Because it must be reported to the state
quiz.why: Airway interventions are the outcome measure for sedation safety, so the record of who needed what and when is the clinical history of that sedation. It is not billed separately, it does not require an order, and routine reporting to the state is not involved.

quiz.q: Which RASS target is appropriate for most sedated emergency department patients?
choices: -4 to -5, so they do not move at all
0 to -2, drowsy but rousable
+1 to +2, so they can communicate freely
-3 to -4, so procedures are not interrupted
quiz.why: Light sedation preserves airway reflexes and respiratory drive and is associated with shorter ventilation and better outcomes. Deeper targets add risk without adding benefit for most procedures, and an agitated positive score is not a sedation target at all.

quiz.q: A patient meets every discharge criterion after sedation except that his ride has cancelled and he wants to take a rideshare home alone. What is correct?
choices: Discharge him, since a rideshare means he is not driving
Have him wait one additional hour and then discharge him alone
Hold discharge until a responsible adult can accompany and observe him, because the requirement is observation, not just transport
Ask him to sign a waiver and discharge him
quiz.why: The criterion exists so that someone can recognize delayed sedation, vomiting or an airway problem at home, which a rideshare driver cannot do. Additional waiting time and a signed waiver do not replace the observation the requirement is for.

quiz.q: Which rapid response call is most likely to get a clinician to the bedside immediately?
choices: "Room 8 seems off to me, can someone check when free?"
"I am worried about the patient in room 8."
"Room 8 might need a doctor at some point."
"ED tech, room 8. Sixty-four-year-old with abdominal pain. Respiratory rate 18 to 28 over forty minutes, systolic 128 down to 88, temp 38.9, newly confused. I need someone at the bedside now."
quiz.why: Naming yourself and the room, the patient, the numbers with their direction, and a direct request leaves nothing to interpret and no room to defer. The other three contain concern without data and a request without a deadline, which is how urgent patients end up in a queue.

quiz.q: You have called a rapid response for a deteriorating patient. What should you do while waiting?
choices: Stay with the patient, get a full set with a counted respiratory rate, bring oxygen and suction to the bedside, confirm IV access, clear the doorway and bring the crash cart outside the room
Go to the supply room to gather equipment that may be needed
Move the patient to a resuscitation bay yourself
Begin charting the event in detail so the record is complete
quiz.why: Everything useful can be done without leaving the bedside, and leaving a deteriorating patient alone is the one thing you cannot undo. Moving a patient single-handed and charting in real time both take attention away from the person who is failing.

quiz.q: During handoff of a monitored patient, which detail is uniquely valuable and most often omitted?
choices: The patient's insurance status
What worries you about this patient
The brand of monitor at the bedside
The time of arrival to the department
quiz.why: Concern is the only element of a handoff that transfers judgment rather than data that is already in the record. It is habitually left out because it feels informal, and it is the sentence that most often changes what the next person watches for.

quiz.q: A patient on continuous observation for suicidal ideation needs to go to radiology, and you are due for a break. What is correct?
choices: Ask the patient to wait quietly until you return
Assume the radiology staff will provide observation
Leave the door open so the hallway staff can see in
Hand the watch to a specifically named person, say it out loud, and get an acknowledgment before you leave
quiz.why: Continuous observation is a named responsibility, not an ambient condition, and it is transferred explicitly with a confirmation back. Assuming another department or passing traffic is watching is precisely how patients on a hold are found down.

scenarios.title: Room 14: the alarm that will not stop
scenarios.intro: You are covering eight monitored beds on an overnight. Room 14 is a `62`-year-old man admitted for chest pain, awaiting a second troponin. His bed has alarmed eleven times in the last two hours, mostly for lead artifact, and the charge nurse has already asked you twice to "do something about 14".

steps.prompt:
The asystole alarm goes off again. From the central station you can see one flat lead and two normal-looking traces.

What do you do?

choices.text: Silence it from the station, since the pattern is identical to the last ten times
choices.feedback: This is the habit that ends careers. The eleventh alarm being artifact does not make the twelfth one artifact, and you have just made a clinical decision about a patient you have not seen.

choices.text: Go to the room, confirm the patient is well, then replace the electrodes and re-prep the skin so the cause is gone
choices.feedback: Right. Going is non-negotiable, and fixing the root cause means the next alarm from this bed will mean something. Fixing a curling electrode is clinical work.

choices.text: Widen the low heart rate limit so asystole will not trigger on this bed
choices.feedback: That is hiding, not adjusting. You have now disabled the alarm that would tell you this man's heart stopped, on a patient here for chest pain.

choices.text: Ask the nurse to come look while you continue with your other beds
choices.feedback: Not unreasonable as an escalation, but you are the person who can see the screen and you are closest. Delegating a thirty-second check adds delay for no benefit.

steps.prompt:
You are in the room. He is awake, talking, slightly sweaty, and says his chest "feels heavy again, but less than before". The flat lead is a curled electrode on his left lower chest. You replace all three, re-prep with alcohol, and leave slack in the cable.

The trace is now clean, showing a regular rhythm at `96`. What else should you do before you leave?

choices.text: Nothing, the trace is fixed and that was the task
choices.feedback: You just heard a patient with chest pain say his chest feels heavy again, and you are about to walk out with that information. The electrode was the errand; the sentence was the finding.

choices.text: Take a full set of vitals and tell the nurse that his chest pain has recurred and he is diaphoretic
choices.feedback: Correct. Recurrent chest pain with diaphoresis in a patient awaiting a second troponin is exactly what the nurse and provider need to know now, not at the next scheduled round.

choices.text: Reassure him that less pain is a good sign and encourage him to rest
choices.feedback: Reassurance is not a plan, and it is not yours to give here. Any recurrence of chest pain is reported, not interpreted at the bedside.

choices.text: Get a full set of vitals and ask whether the team wants a repeat 12-lead ECG, then tell the nurse
choices.feedback: Good. Recurrent pain is a standard trigger for a repeat ECG in most departments, and offering it while you report saves a step.

steps.prompt:
Twenty minutes later a different alarm from room 14: heart rate `188`. You look at the screen and see a wide, regular, rapid complex. You reach the room in ten seconds. He is pale, clammy, and answers you slowly.

What is your read?

choices.text: Motion artifact; he has been restless all night
choices.feedback: The patient contradicts you. He is pale, clammy, hypotensive and slow to answer, which is a patient matching the number. Motion artifact does not drop a blood pressure.

choices.text: A real wide-complex tachycardia in a patient who looks unwell; call for help now and stay in the room
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Wide, fast and unwell together is the combination treated as real before anything else, and it is one of the alarms you never rationalize away.

choices.text: Double counting of tall T waves; verify the rate by feeling a pulse first
choices.feedback: Feeling a pulse is a good habit, but not instead of calling for help in a hypotensive, pale patient. Do both, and put the call first.

choices.text: Silence the alarm so you can concentrate, then go find the nurse
choices.feedback: Two errors in one. Silencing removes the signal that brings others, and leaving the room takes the only person watching him out of it.

steps.prompt:
The nurse and the physician arrive within a minute. The rhythm is treated and converts. The patient's pressure comes up and he is moved to a resuscitation bay. The charge nurse, who asked you twice to "do something about 14", comes to find you.

What is the lesson you take from the eleven false alarms?

choices.text: That most alarms are false, so the real skill is knowing when to ignore them
choices.feedback: This is exactly the conclusion that gets patients killed. The skill is not ignoring alarms, it is removing the false ones so the real one is answered.

choices.text: That every false alarm left unfixed makes the next real alarm less likely to be answered, so fixing causes at the source is clinical work
choices.feedback: That is the lesson. Eleven unfixed alarms had trained an entire team to look away from bed 14, which is precisely how alarm fatigue harms people.

choices.text: That alarm limits on this bed should have been widened hours earlier
choices.feedback: Widening limits would have removed the asystole alarm and the tachycardia alarm together. The problem was never the limits; it was the electrodes.

choices.text: That documenting the alarm history and what you fixed at handoff would have helped the whole team trust bed 14 again
choices.feedback: A genuinely useful addition. Saying "I changed his electrodes at 0210 because the lead kept dropping" tells the next person the alarm history is clean from that point.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern here is alarm fatigue doing exactly what it is known to do. Eleven artifact alarms had taught a department that bed 14 cries wolf, and the twelfth alarm was a wide-complex tachycardia in a hypotensive man with recurrent chest pain.

Three habits carried this case. Going to the bedside every time, because the previous ten alarms tell you nothing about this one. Fixing the cause at the source rather than silencing or widening, so the noise actually goes away. And noticing the patient rather than the errand: the most important information in the entire scenario was a sentence the patient said while you were changing an electrode.

The last step matters too. The wrong lesson from a night like this is that alarms are mostly noise. The right lesson is that noise is a fixable problem, and that fixing it is how the next real alarm gets answered.

scenarios.title: Room 2: 71-year-old with flank pain and a fever
scenarios.intro: Triage hands you a `71`-year-old woman brought in by her daughter for two days of right flank pain, fever and vomiting. She has diabetes and takes metformin. She looks tired and is answering questions slowly but appropriately. You are taking her first set of vital signs.

steps.prompt:
You get: heart rate `104`, blood pressure `108/64`, oral temperature `37.6 C`, SpO2 `96%` on room air. The monitor shows a respiratory rate of `17`. She feels warm to you and her skin is dry.

What do you do about the numbers?

choices.text: Chart them as obtained; nothing crosses a threshold
choices.feedback: Two of those numbers are not measurements. The monitor's respiratory rate is derived from chest impedance, and an oral temperature in a vomiting, dehydrated patient underestimates. You may have just failed to start a sepsis clock.

choices.text: Count the respiratory rate yourself for a full minute and repeat the temperature by a more reliable route
choices.feedback: Correct. You count `24`, and a rectal temperature reads `38.7 C`. That changes the picture from borderline to two SIRS criteria plus a source, which is a sepsis alert.

choices.text: Recheck the blood pressure only, since that is the number closest to a threshold
choices.feedback: Reasonable instinct, wrong target. The blood pressure is the one number here that is probably accurate. The respiratory rate and temperature are the two most likely to be wrong and the two that would change the plan.

choices.text: Report the tachycardia and wait for the nurse to decide what else to check
choices.feedback: Reporting is good, but waiting is not. Counting a respiratory rate takes sixty seconds and a rectal temperature takes two minutes, and both are yours to do.

steps.prompt:
You report: temp `38.7 C`, heart rate `104`, counted respiratory rate `24`, systolic `108`, and she is slower than her daughter says is normal. The nurse activates the sepsis pathway. The provider orders the hour-1 bundle.

You have the room to yourself for the next four minutes. What do you do first?

choices.text: Start one `22 gauge` IV in the hand and draw the labs from it
choices.feedback: That catheter cannot deliver `30 mL/kg` in the time the bundle intends. A septic patient needs two large-bore lines, `18 gauge` or bigger, and hand veins are the last resort.

choices.text: Place two `18 gauge` IVs, draw blood cultures from two sites plus the lactate and labs, and get the fluid ready to hang
choices.feedback: Exactly the right order of work. Access first, cultures before antibiotics, lactate in the same draw, and fluid primed so nothing waits on you.

choices.text: Hang the antibiotics as soon as pharmacy sends them, and draw cultures afterward when there is time
choices.feedback: Cultures drawn after antibiotics often fail to grow the organism, which costs the team the ability to narrow therapy later. Two minutes of culture draw is not a meaningful delay.

choices.text: Place two large-bore IVs and draw everything, and ask whether they want a urinary catheter for hourly output measurement
choices.feedback: Good, and the catheter question is the right one for a patient whose urine output will be a marker of response over the next few hours.

steps.prompt:
Antibiotics are in at the `42` minute mark. The lactate resulted at `4.1 mmol/L`, so she gets the full `30 mL/kg`. She weighs `62 kg`.

How much fluid is that, and how does it run?

choices.text: About `620 mL` by gravity through the smaller line
choices.feedback: That is `10 mL/kg`, a third of what is ordered, and gravity through a small line will not deliver it fast enough either.

choices.text: About `1860 mL`, run through large-bore access under a pressure bag or rapid infuser
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. `30 mL/kg` times `62 kg` is roughly `1860 mL`, and it is meant to go in quickly, which is why the large-bore access you placed matters now.

choices.text: About `1860 mL`, run over the next six hours so she does not develop pulmonary edema
choices.feedback: The volume is right and the timing is wrong. Slow delivery in the resuscitation window is under-resuscitation. Concerns about overload are managed by reassessing, not by running the bundle dose over six hours.

choices.text: About `3100 mL`, since older patients need more
choices.feedback: That is `50 mL/kg` and it is not the bundle dose. Inventing a larger volume in a 71-year-old with diabetes is its own harm.

steps.prompt:
It is now two hours since the clock started. The fluid is in. Her blood pressure is `102/60`, heart rate `108`. She has become much quieter and does not object when you take her arm for a blood pressure. Her daughter says "she is finally comfortable, she must be feeling better".

What do you think?

choices.text: Agree; the fluids and antibiotics are working and she is settling
choices.feedback: Her heart rate did not fall, her respiratory rate did not fall, and her mentation changed. Improvement lowers the heart rate. This is the falling-agitation pattern, and it is deterioration.

choices.text: Treat new quietness with a persistently high heart rate as worsening perfusion, and report it now with the repeat lactate
choices.feedback: Correct, and the reassessment items are exactly what is due at this point: a repeat lactate, the urine output total, and a hands-on perfusion check.

choices.text: Give her some time to rest and recheck at the next scheduled interval
choices.feedback: The next scheduled interval is too late for a change in mental status in a septic patient. This is the moment the reassessment exists for.

choices.text: Check her capillary refill, knee temperature and skin for mottling before deciding, then report what you find
choices.feedback: Good instinct. Hands-on perfusion signs change before numbers do in both directions, and they turn your concern into something concrete to report.

steps.prompt:
The repeat lactate is `5.2 mmol/L`, up from `4.1`. Her knees are mottled and capillary refill at the chest is `4 seconds`. Norepinephrine is started and she is accepted to the ICU. You are giving handoff to the ICU nurse.

What is the item most likely to be left out, and most needed?

choices.text: Her home medication list
choices.feedback: Important, and it is already in the record. It is not what the receiving team cannot reconstruct without you.

choices.text: The timeline: when the clock started, the exact antibiotic time, how much of the `1860 mL` actually infused, both lactate values with times, and the urine output total
choices.feedback: Exactly. A bag hung is not a bag infused, and the ICU plans the next hours from these numbers. This is the part that lives only in your head.

choices.text: The name of the provider who saw her
choices.feedback: Easily looked up and rarely the thing that changes management. Hand off what cannot be retrieved from the chart.

choices.text: That the daughter thought she was improving
choices.feedback: Family observations matter, but this one was wrong and reporting it as reassurance could mislead. What belongs in handoff is the objective finding: she became quiet while her heart rate stayed up.

scenarios.debrief:
This case turns twice, and both turns belong to the technician.

The first is the opening set of vital signs. A guessed respiratory rate of 17 and an oral temperature of 37.6 in a vomiting, vasoconstricted patient would have left her looking borderline, and the sepsis clock would have started whenever somebody else noticed. A counted rate of 24 and a core temperature of 38.7 started it at triage.

The second is the quiet patient at two hours. Falling agitation with a persistently high heart rate is a brain running out of perfusion, and it is one of the most reliably misread findings in emergency medicine, especially when a family member offers you the comfortable interpretation first.

Underneath both is arithmetic: 30 mL/kg is a real number that has to be calculated from a real weight and delivered through access that can carry it, and the amount that actually infused is the number the next team needs most.

scenarios.title: Room 6: 14-month-old, two days of cough
scenarios.intro: A `14`-month-old boy is brought in by both parents for two days of cough and poor feeding. Triage recorded a heart rate of `168`, respiratory rate `56`, temperature `38.1 C`, SpO2 `93%` on room air, weight `10 kg`. He is in his mother's arms, crying intermittently. You are assigned to get him on the monitor.

steps.prompt:
You walk in. He is crying, arching away from you, and his mother looks exhausted.

What is your first move?

choices.text: Lay him on the stretcher and apply all the leads and the probe quickly so the numbers are captured
choices.feedback: You will get motion artifact on the pleth, a fictional impedance respiratory rate and a blood pressure taken mid-scream. A fighting child produces numbers nobody can use.

choices.text: Watch him from the doorway for fifteen seconds first: appearance, work of breathing, and color, before you touch anything
choices.feedback: The pediatric assessment triangle, and it costs fifteen seconds. You see nasal flaring, subcostal retractions and a child who still tracks his mother, which tells you more than the first set of numbers will.

choices.text: Leave him with his parents and come back when he has settled on his own
choices.feedback: A child working this hard does not get left to settle. Observation is the point, and you can do it without touching him.

choices.text: Apply the SpO2 probe to a finger and get that number before doing anything else
choices.feedback: The probe goes on a toe or a wrapped foot in a child this age, and grabbing a hand first is the fastest way to lose his cooperation for everything that follows.

steps.prompt:
He has nasal flaring, subcostal and intercostal retractions, and a wet cough. He is still interactive with his mother. You want real numbers.

How do you get them?

choices.text: Keep him on his mother's chest, put the probe on a toe, count the respiratory rate by watching his abdomen, and save the blood pressure for last
choices.feedback: This is how you get data worth charting. Comfort is measurement technique in pediatrics, and counting by watching beats any impedance number the monitor will give you.

choices.text: Swaddle him tightly including the arms so he cannot move during the readings
choices.feedback: Tight swaddling of a child in respiratory distress restricts the chest movement he is depending on. Comfort holds on a parent, not restraint.

choices.text: Take the numbers from the triage set and recheck in an hour
choices.feedback: A child in visible distress needs current numbers, and the triage set is already thirty minutes old on a patient who can change fast.

choices.text: Get the probe and the leads on while a parent holds and distracts him, and accept that the blood pressure may need a second attempt
choices.feedback: Practical and correct. Parent-assisted positioning plus realistic expectations about the blood pressure gets you usable numbers without a fight.

steps.prompt:
Settled on his mother's chest you get: heart rate `172`, respiratory rate counted at `58`, SpO2 `91%` on room air, capillary refill at the chest `3 seconds`, blood pressure `88/54`.

How do you report this?

choices.text: As stable, since the blood pressure is normal for a toddler
choices.feedback: The blood pressure is the last number to fail in a child and it tells you almost nothing here. Tachycardia, tachypnea, delayed central refill and hypoxemia together are a sick child.

choices.text: As a child in respiratory distress with early compensated shock: rate `172`, respirations `58` with flaring and retractions, saturation `91%`, central refill `3 seconds`
choices.feedback: Correct, and reporting the work of breathing alongside the numbers is what makes it actionable. The normal blood pressure is not reassurance, it is the compensation still holding.

choices.text: As a mild viral illness needing observation and oral fluids
choices.feedback: Flaring, retractions and a saturation of 91 are not mild. Undercalling this is how a child ends up deteriorating in a waiting room.

choices.text: With the numbers plus the specific findings the parents can confirm: he has not fed since last night and has had two wet diapers in 24 hours
choices.feedback: A strong addition. Feeding and wet diapers are the most useful perfusion history available in a toddler and they belong in the same sentence as the vitals.

steps.prompt:
He is started on oxygen and suctioned, and the team is preparing further treatment. Forty minutes later you glance over: he has stopped crying, he is limp against his mother, and the monitor shows a heart rate of `76`.

What is this?

choices.text: Improvement; the oxygen and suctioning have worked and he has fallen asleep
choices.feedback: His saturation fell, his tone is gone and his rate more than halved. Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise, and this is the step immediately before arrest.

choices.text: A pre-arrest state: bradycardia in a child is hypoxia, and it needs help in the room now with airway and ventilation
choices.feedback: Exactly. Children compensate with tachycardia until they run out of oxygen, at which point the rate crashes. Call out loud, get help, and support the airway immediately.

choices.text: Probable artifact; reposition the probe and leads and recheck
choices.feedback: The patient matches the number: limp, quiet, desaturating. Troubleshooting equipment on a floppy hypoxic infant costs the minutes you do not have.

choices.text: A vagal response to the suctioning a few minutes ago; call for help while you reassess
choices.feedback: Suctioning can provoke bradycardia, so it is a reasonable thought, but the response is the same and the help still comes first. Never leave a floppy bradycardic child to declare itself.

steps.prompt:
Help arrives in seconds. He is ventilated with a bag-valve-mask, his heart rate comes up to `150` within a minute, tone returns, and he begins to cry again. He is admitted to the pediatric ICU.

What is the single most transferable lesson?

choices.text: That blood pressure is the most reliable indicator of shock in children
choices.feedback: The opposite. In children the heart rate tells the truth and the blood pressure holds until it suddenly does not. His pressure was normal an hour before he nearly arrested.

choices.text: That bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise, and that a child who goes quiet after working hard has usually got worse, not better
choices.feedback: That is the lesson, and both halves of it were live in this case. Ventilation, not compressions, was what fixed him, because hypoxia was the cause.

choices.text: That equipment artifact is the most common cause of alarming pediatric numbers
choices.feedback: Artifact is common in upset children, which is exactly why you settle the child and get real numbers. It is not a reason to disbelieve a limp, desaturating infant.

choices.text: That comfort positioning and parental involvement produced usable data at every step of this case
choices.feedback: True and worth keeping. Every accurate number in this case came from a child held on a parent's chest rather than pinned to a stretcher.

scenarios.debrief:
Children compensate beautifully and then fall off a cliff, and this case walks the whole edge of it. Every number that mattered came from a child settled on a parent rather than fought with on a stretcher, which is why comfort is described here as measurement technique rather than kindness.

The assessment triangle did the early work: appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin identified a sick child before a single lead went on. The reporting step is the one to practise, because a normal blood pressure in a tachycardic, tachypneic toddler with delayed central refill is not reassurance, it is compensation that has not failed yet.

The last turn is the one to memorize. A quiet, floppy child with a heart rate that has halved is not resting. Bradycardia in a child is hypoxia until proven otherwise, and the treatment is oxygen and ventilation, delivered immediately.
